articles.title: Diplomatic visits attempt to hold off all-out US-Iran war
articles.body:
We're closing this live page now.
Join us back here from 0700 tomorrow for more live coverage of developments in the Middle East.
Thanks for following.
Welcome,
Here are the key updates:
And so we continue our live coverage of the day...
Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian has held talks with Pakistan's army chief Asim Munir in Tehran amid renewed efforts to mediate an end to the US-Iran war.
The two leaders discussed ongoing mediation efforts and regional developments, Iran's Nour News reports.
The New Arab reported earlier that Munir delivered a new peace proposal to Iranian officials, which Pakistan and Qatar hope will prevent renewed conflict between Iran and the US and get the two sides to return to the negotiating table.
A drone strike by the Sudanese army killed 53 people at a market in an area disputed between Sudan and South Sudan, local authorities said on Tuesday, the latest in a wave of deadly attacks.
Authorities in Abyei district said the strike hit Amiet market on Monday. They accused the army of launching 22 munitions during the attack, which also wounded at least 27 people.
"The casualties comprise vulnerable civilian populations, including women, children, the elderly, local merchants, members of the host Ngok Dinka community, South Sudanese returnees, and Sudanese refugees who had sought sanctuary from the broader regional conflict," the authorities said.
On Sunday and Monday, strikes across Sudan killed more than 100 people. The country is in the grips of a brutal war between the regular army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) that began in April 2023.
Local Yemeni authorities on Tuesday raised the death toll from a Houthi strike a day earlier on a military camp belonging to government forces to 73, as fighting between the foes escalates.
It marked the deadliest attack in weeks as fighting between the Iran-backed Houthis and Yemen's internationally recognised, Saudi-supported government rages after the collapse of a years-long truce.
The death toll from Monday's strike on the camp in the energy-rich Shabwa province "increased to 73 martyrs, while search and follow-up efforts are ongoing to discover the fate of 14 missing people", provincial authorities said in a statement.
Local authorities had put the death toll at 53 on Monday, adding that more than 200 others were injured, all new members of the internal security forces who were undergoing training.
Majed al-Nuzaili, spokesperson for the Yemeni armed forces, stated Monday on X that the Houthis targeted Shabwa with three ballistic missiles, and that the attack "struck a training center for personnel of security and police agencies."
The head of the International Energy Agency said Tuesday that he saw little chance of a return to normal oil market conditions next year, as the ongoing wars in the Middle East region keeps prices high.
"I personally don't see any credible pathway that 2027 will be a year of normalisation" after the Gulf supply disruptions caused by the US and Israeli attacks on Iran last February, Fatih Birol told a conference organised by The Financial Times.
The war sparked by the attacks has sent oil prices to over $100 a barrel compared with below $70 a barrel before hostilities began, while damage to Gulf refineries has helped push diesel prices to record highs.
In response, the IEA has organised the release of up to 400 million barrels of oil in strategic reserves held by member countries, and Birol said further releases could be made if warranted.
Iran has vowed to take control of tanker shipments through the Strait of Hormuz, which has driven up transport insurance costs even though flows have reportedly returned to prewar levels in recent weeks.
"If there's an overlapping crisis in the Middle East, I cannot exclude that our governments will look at the other options," Birol told the FT's Energy Transition conference.
"It's a big thing, 400 million barrels, but it's only 20 percent of the oil we have—80 percent is in the pocket," he said.
Sources familiar with mediation efforts told The New Arab that Qatar and Pakistan presented a "middle-ground proposal" that meets the demands of both the US and Iranian sides.
Sources added that the proposal brought today by the Pakistani army chief to Iranian officials has US approval and had already received prior Iranian approval.
The proposal offers around $6 billion, which are Iranian funds frozen in banks in Qatar, as a "partial response" to Iran's demand to recover the frozen funds.
The proposal responds to a US demand regarding Iran’s nuclear file, as Iran apparently agreed to a secret visit by the International Atomic Energy Agency to its nuclear sites.
Turkey will keep its own troops in Syria and Iraq until border security with its two neighbours has been fully ensured, Defence Minister Yasar Guler told AFP in an interview.
"We are maintaining our military presence in Iraq and Syria. When we assess that the necessary conditions have been met in terms of regional and border security, the status of our base areas and our presence in the region will be reconsidered," he said in a written answer to AFP questions.
Iran's ambassador to Iraq said on Tuesday that Baghdad had agreed to "expel" or hand over members of Iranian Kurdish opposition groups who have taken refuge on the Iraqi side of the border.
The announcement came after senior Iraqi security officials repeatedly told AFP that Baghdad was refusing to do so, fearing for the lives of the Kurdish exiles.
Iraq's autonomous Kurdistan region, an oil-rich area in the north of the country, has long hosted camps and bases for Iranian Kurdish rebel groups, which Tehran labels terrorists who serve US or Israeli interests.
"During a meeting of the joint security commission—attended by the Iranian delegation and the Iraqi National Security Adviser—the two parties agreed to expel the members of the Iranian separatist terrorist groups from the Iraqi Kurdistan region or hand them over to Iran," ambassador Mohammad Kazem Al-Sadegh wrote on X.
The United Nations insisted Tuesday that aid must immediately be allowed to enter Yemen's third-biggest city Taiz, besieged by pro-Iran Houthi fighters blocking all supplies.
"Humanitarian aid must be immediately allowed to enter the city and its passage must be facilitated," UN rights chief Volker Turk said in a statement, warning that civilians were being placed "at grave risk".
Turkey has submitted a defence pact with Pakistan and Saudi Arabia to parliament for ratification, three parliamentary sources said on Tuesday, moving NATO's second-largest army closer to a formal mutual defence pledge with Riyadh as it faces Houthi attacks.
The three countries signed the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement in August, under which an armed attack on one member is considered an attack on all. A joint statement issued when they signed the deal did not specify what each country had committed to.
At an emergency meeting of the alliance in Riyadh earlier this month, they agreed to ensure the "rapid deployment" of military forces and capabilities in Saudi Arabia.
Turkey, which has a robust defence industry, has condemned Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, expressed willingness to help meet Riyadh's military technology needs and agreed to join a Saudi-led coalition to ensure navigational safety in the Red Sea.
Parliamentary ratification is required for Turkey to formally approve the agreement.
French President Emmanuel Macron has secured the delivery of an additional 200,000 tonnes of diesel per month from the United Arab Emirates and Bahrain during a tour of the Gulf, the French presidency said Tuesday.
He obtained commitments for around 100,000 tonnes per month from the Emirates, while an additional 100,000 tonnes monthly will be secured during a stop in Bahrain later in the day, the Elysee Palace said.
With the addition of deliveries from Saudi Arabia, France has commitments for 295,000 tonnes per month, representing just over 10 percent of its consumption, the presidency added.
Macron is undertaking a tour of key energy suppliers in the Gulf in an effort to secure oil and diesel supplies and bring down prices in France, after a weekend of violent protests sparked by soaring living costs.
He is visiting the UAE, Bahrain and Qatar, all of which have been thrown into turmoil since February by the US-Iran war.
Israeli strikes and gunfire killed at least four Palestinians, including a married couple and a 17-year-old, in separate incidents in the Gaza Strip on Tuesday, health officials said.
Medics said an Israeli airstrike killed Akram Yassin and his wife Dina Abu Baker in an apartment in Gaza City.
The Israeli military said it struck a militant in the area, without giving further details.
In Khan Younis, in the south, medics said a 17-year-old boy was killed by Israeli gunfire near the Qizan Al-Najar neighbourhood, while another was killed by Israeli gunfire in the Zeitoun suburb east of Gaza City, taking Tuesday's death toll to at least four.
Britain will deploy Royal Air Force fighter jets on defensive missions to help protect Saudi Arabia from escalating Houthi attacks, Bloomberg reported on Tuesday, citing British officials familiar with the matter.
RAF Typhoon fighter jets will help defend Saudi cities and infrastructure against aerial attacks by the Iran-backed group, while Britain will also provide an Atlas A400M transport aircraft and military advisers, the report said.
Britain's Ministry of Defence did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Iran has deliberately prolonged talks with the US to try to weaken Donald Trump politically ahead of November's US midterm elections, senior officials say, while fears of renewed military action and deep distrust of Washington have reinforced Tehran's reluctance to strike a quick deal to end the war.
Three senior Iranian officials and an Iranian insider, speaking on condition of anonymity, said Tehran was convinced the US president was ready to resort to renewed attacks to try to break the stalemate in the eight-month-old war.
"Iran is preparing for renewed Israeli and US attacks, not for a deal with America to end the war," one of the officials said. "The clerical establishment is determined not to give Trump a political victory."
The United Nations reported on Tuesday that the estimated number of displaced people has become more than 250,000 inside Yemen since the resumption of hostilities.
The death toll from a Houthi missile strike on a government military camp in southern Yemen rose to 60 people, primarily new recruits, making it the deadliest strike since fighting in the country erupted three months ago, Yemeni officials said Tuesday.
At least a dozen people were still missing a day after the Iranian-backed rebels hit the al-Alam training camp in the southern province of Shabwa with ballistic missiles, three officials said.
Monday's strike was part of a recent surge of fighting in Yemen, which started when forces from the internationally-recognized government and Saudi-led coalition launched airstrikes on Houthi-held Sanaa International Airport in July, shattering a 2022 ceasefire deal that largely stopped fighting in the country's civil war.
Two tankers were set ablaze and brought to a halt south of the Strait of Hormuz after hitting Iranian mines, the Revolutionary Guards' Navy said in a statement shared by state media on Tuesday, without saying when the tankers were hit.
The statement also said a US drone was downed by Iran on Monday night.
Saudi forces on Tuesday intercepted a ballistic missile aimed at the kingdom's capital, said a spokesman for the Riyadh-led coalition backing Yemen's government, after authorities issued a danger warning and AFP journalists reported hearing blasts.
The kingdom "intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile launched by the terrorist Houthi militia towards Riyadh", Turki Al-Malki said in a post on X.
The Saudi capital on Tuesday was shaken by two blasts, according to AFP journalists, after authorities issued an alert warning of potential danger.
"A warning has been issued by the National Early Warning Platform in Riyadh City to alert for a potential danger," the Saudi civil defence said in a statement on X.
Iran shot down an American drone over the Strait of Hormuz at dawn today, according to Tasnim.
A statement by Iran's Revolutionary Guard stated that the fifty-fourth US Army MQ9 drone was intercepted and destroyed in the airspace of the Strait of Hormuz, by modern advanced air defense system of the Revolutionary Guard’s air-space force, and under the guidance of the country’s integrated air defense network.
Brent crude futures increased by 52 cents, or 0.47 percent, reaching $110.07.
The US West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude contract for November delivery, which expired Tuesday, climbed 0.36 percent to $104.03 per barrel.
Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis said on Monday they carried out several attacks against Saudi energy, airport and military targets, including an Aramco site in Yanbu, the Shaybah oilfield, King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh and Abha airport.
There was no immediate Saudi confirmation and Reuters could not immediately verify the claims.
Pakistan's army chief, General Asim Munir, is due to arrive in Tehran today, Tuesday, Iran's semi-official Tasnim news agency reported.
There was no Pakistani confirmation of the visit.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Tuesday that Russia and Iran have "never" worked so closely, as Moscow seeks to play a mediating role in the Middle East war.
Araghchi hosted his Russian counterpart Sergey Lavrov in Iran on Monday, in his first visit since the outbreak of the conflict.
"We covered everything from Europe to West Asia, including Lebanon, Palestine, Ukraine and Yemen. Also focused on expansion of economic and nuclear cooperation," Araghchi wrote on X.
"Never in our history have Iran and Russia worked as closely as now."
Lavrov said ahead of the visit that Moscow's efforts "aimed at preventing the return of a large-scale war", with talks stalled between the United States and Iran.
His visit came after Russian President Vladimir Putin told his Iranian counterpart Masoud Pezeshkian this month that Moscow was prepared to contribute to mediation efforts.

articles.title: Zelensky in Oslo for talks with US envoys as Ukraine claims missile holdup
articles.body:
Ukraine ‘losing people and time’, Zelensky says after Oslo talks
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has wrapped up talks with US envoys in Norway Tuesday where he was determined to put diplomacy back on a "more constructive path”, Oslo officials said. Zelensky told a post-meeting press briefing that Ukraine was not losing the war but was “losing people and time” saying he was hopeful moving forward because “we have some clear ideas of how to get peace”.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky held talks in Oslo on Tuesday with top US envoys in a bid to get strained relations with Washington "on a more constructive path", Oslo said.
Following the talks, the Ukrainian leader told a press briefing that although Ukraine was not losing the war it was “losing people and time”.
He also emphasised that Ukraine should be “at the table” in any upcoming trilateral talks between the US, Russia and China.
"I don't know what the trilateral meeting will be about between America and China, and Russia, it's up to them. But of course, if the are issues about Ukraine, our future, it can be acceptable only when we are at the table of negotiations. It's absolutely clear," Zelensky told reporters.
Donald Trump's envoy Steve Witkoff is to visit Russia on Wednesday, a source told TASS state news agency.
Zelensky added he was thankful that US intelligence sharing had resumed.
"We are thankful that intelligence works... I'm speaking about early warning, what is very important for our people, for children, adults, civilians, because we can hear when ballistic is coming," Zelensky told reporters in Oslo.
Earlier, Zelensky had accused the United States of deliberately withholding vital intelligence and delaying military aid, saying on Monday that Ukraine received no early warning of powerful Russian missile strikes that targeted energy facilities in the capital region.
Read moreWhy have US-Ukraine relations soured ahead of the midterms?
Witkoff's fellow US envoy Jared Kushner -- US President Donald Trump's son-in-law -- was also taking part in the negotiations but was doing so remotely because of illness, according to the NTB agency.
Relations between Kyiv and Washington have soured since Trump partially lifted sanctions to strike a diesel-supply deal with Russia's Vladimir Putin and slammed Zelensky as a warmonger for Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil refineries.

US-led diplomatic efforts to end Europe's deadliest conflict since World War II have stalled in recent months, as Washington has shifted focus towards the war with Iran.
"The aim is to put diplomatic efforts on a more constructive path," he said.
'Needed to protect lives'
Ahead of the meeting, Zelensky on Tuesday said he held "substantive" and "constructive" talks with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, in which he insisted that the US military satellite system Ukraine uses, Starshield, "needs to be restored" and that ballistic missile interceptors "are needed to protect lives".
Zelensky told US senators on Monday that "the Pentagon is delaying the delivery of missiles" already paid for by European countries, and that the shipment was waiting for US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth's signature.
He said several European countries were ready to transfer Patriot interceptor missiles from their own stockpiles but were still awaiting US approval.
The US has denied making any changes to intelligence sharing with Ukraine, and Rubio on Tuesday said Washington was not deliberately withholding supplies.
"There's nothing being deliberately denied to Ukraine," Rubio said while on a trip to India.
"It's simply, it's a balance between our obligations to other partners and frankly our own ... requirements for our own facilities as well."
Read moreWill Trump really pull the plug? Starlink restored but Ukraine's fate still uncertain
Trump has also denied ordering a reduction in speeds on the US government-owned and -controlled Starshield network after Elon Musk, whose company SpaceX developed it, said the order could only have come from the White House.
Strained relations
The US leader has accused his counterpart of not trying to resolve the conflict with Russia.
"Zelensky doesn't know what he's talking about," Trump said on Monday.
"To be honest, I think it's time for somebody else to negotiate on behalf of Ukraine."
Trump said he was ready to meet Putin and Chinese leader Xi Jinping in China next month to discuss denuclearisation, adding that talks could also cover the Ukraine war – fuelling fears in Kyiv that it was being sidelined.

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov confirmed earlier that "the topic of such a hypothetical has indeed been mentioned" when asked about a Wall Street Journal report on Sunday that Trump, Putin and Xi could meet.
Ukraine's Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiga said that such a meeting would "only encourage Putin to continue this war".
News outlet Axios reported that Witkoff would travel from Oslo to Russia to meet Putin.
"We hope that it will be possible to arrange a meeting in the very near future, allowing the American negotiators... Mr Witkoff, to brief President Putin on their contacts with both the Ukrainians and the Europeans," Peskov told reporters Tuesday.
Ukrainian authorities said Tuesday that Russian strikes killed at least six people around the country, as Moscow targets energy and transport infrastructure with winter approaching.
The attacks came after Zelensky said Kyiv would resume hitting Russian refineries in the face of unrelenting strikes, more than four and a half years into the war.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

articles.title: Ukraine war latest: Drone strikes on Yandex data centers disrupt Russian court hearings, media reports
articles.body:
Ukraine war latest: Drone strikes on Yandex data centers disrupt Russian court hearings, media reports
Key developments on Oct. 20:
- Ukrainian strikes on Yandex data centers disrupt Russian court hearings, media reports
- Ukraine's HUR claims 108 Russian soldiers killed, 29 captured in Sumy Oblast operation
- Power outages in half of Ukraine's oblasts after Russian assault on power plants
- Fire at oil pumping station in Russia’s Tambov Oblast after drone attack, monitoring channels say
- Poland has no Patriot missiles left for Ukraine, Sikorski says
- Russian drones strike Kyiv hospital, injure 5 across the city
Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian tech giant Yandex's data centers disrupted dozens of court hearings across Russia, independent Russian media outlet Verstka reported on Oct. 16.
The disruptions come as Moscow and Kyiv increasingly target each other's data centers.
Russian courts began canceling hearings on Oct. 8, following a Ukrainian strike on one of Yandex's largest data centers in Sasovo, Ryazan Oblast. PravoTech, the company responsible for maintaining Russia's electronic arbitration court system, subsequently reported a major outage at a Yandex Cloud data center.
The disruptions affected courts across several Russian regions, including Sverdlovsk, Smolensk, Tula, Kostroma, Ivanovo, and Yaroslavl oblasts. Courts were unable to hold online hearings, record audio and video, or access documents through the electronic court system, the Moscow Times reported.
Russia intensified its attacks on Ukraine's digital infrastructure in September. On Sept. 23, a Russian strike damaged a Kyiv data center, disrupting internet access for around 100,000 households and affecting cloud services.
Ukraine responded with strikes on three Yandex data centers, a Sberbank facility under construction, and a data center operated by Russian social media giant VK between Oct. 8 and 18. Most recently, on Oct. 20, Ukrainian forces reportedly destroyed another data center in Donetsk Oblast.
read also
Ukraine's HUR claims 108 Russian soldiers killed, 29 captured in Sumy Oblast operation
Ukrainian special forces killed 108 Russian soldiers, captured another 29, and struck more than 1,100 Russian targets during a seven-week operation in Sumy Oblast, Ukraine's military intelligence (HUR) reported on Oct. 20.
According to HUR's Active Operations Department, the operation was carried out by its Group 10 special forces unit, which reportedly thwarted Russian offensive plans and prevented Russian troops from cutting off Ukrainian logistical routes in the region.
Over the course of seven weeks, Ukrainian operatives cleared Russian troops from more than 600 hectares of forest before handing over the positions to Ukraine's Defense Forces, the intelligence agency said.
HUR did not specify the exact location of the operation or when it took place.
The Kyiv Independent could not independently verify these claims.
Ukraine's defensive operations reduced the pace of Russia's territorial advances by more than half in the first six months of 2026, then-Commander-in-Chief Oleksandr Syrskyi said on July 10.
Separately, on Sept. 28, Ukraine's 3rd Army Corps reported further territorial gains in northern Donetsk Oblast as part of Operation Vivaldi, a counteroffensive that had reclaimed a total of 176 square kilometers. According to the corps, the latest phase of the operation inflicted more than 2,000 Russian casualties and resulted in the capture of over 250 Russian soldiers.
read also
Power outages in half of Ukraine's oblasts after Russian assault on power plants
Due to Russian attacks, Ukraine's state-owned electricity operator reported power outages in twelve of Ukraine's oblasts on Oct. 20.
"There are new power outages in the Kirovohrad, Zhytomyr, Lviv, Odesa, Rivne, Ternopil, Khmelnytskyi, Zaporizhia, Donetsk, Kharkiv, Sumy and Chernihiv oblasts in the morning," Ukrenergo said.
To avoid overloading previously damaged equipment, power limitation schedules for industry will be applied across all of Ukraine, as well as hourly outage schedules in some oblasts, according to the operator.
Russia continues to "systematically and purposefully attack" Ukraine's energy sector, Ukrainian First Deputy Minister of Energy of Artem Nekrasov said in a briefing on Oct. 20.
"At night and in the morning, Russia attacked energy facilities in Kirovohrad, Zhytomyr, Lviv, Odessa, Rivne, Ternopil and Khmelnytsky Oblasts," Nekrasov said, adding that due to the Russian strikes some consumers were left without power supply.
The strikes come as Russia intensifies its drone and missile campaign against Ukrainian energy infrastructure as the country approaches its fifth winter since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022.
The day before, another wave of Russian missile and drone strikes had hit 28 electrical substations and other critical energy facilities across Ukraine, President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Oct. 19.
16 ballistic missiles and over 200 drones were used in what Zelensky described as a "targeted attack on Kyiv and Kyiv Oblast."
Fire at oil pumping station in Russia’s Tambov Oblast after drone attack, monitoring channels say
A fire reportedly broke out at an oil pumping station near the Russian city of Michurinsk in Tambov Oblast after an overnight drone attack on Oct. 20, according to Telegram monitoring channels.
Tambov Oblast governor Yevgeny Pervyshov said that a Ukrainian drone attack caused a fire "on the territory of one of the enterprises" in Michurinsky District but did not specify at which facility. He claimed that four drones in total were shot down overnight and in the morning of Oct. 20, mainly by mobile fire groups. He reported no casualties.
On video footage of the reported attack published by monitoring channel Exilenova+, a fire and dark smoke can be seen at what residents supposedly identified as a diesel fuel tank.
Independent Russian outlet ASTRA said the fire likely started at the Nikolskoye-1 linear production and dispatch station near the village of Novonikolskoye.
The Nikolskoye linear production and dispatch station is a major oil and petroleum facility, operated by Transneft as part of the Druzhba oil pipeline network. The station is located about 350 to 400 kilometers (about 220 to 250 miles) from the frontline in Ukraine.
Ukrainian authorities did not yet confirm an attack. The Kyiv Independent could not independently verify a fire at the station.
Ukraine attacked the station previously on Aug. 18, 2025. Robert "Madyar" Brovdi, who heads Ukraine's Unmanned Systems Forces, then confirmed that drones of the 14th Regiment of the Unmanned Systems Unit attacked the Nikolskoye oil pumping station, which halted the operation of the Russian Druzhba oil pipeline.
The Druzhba pipeline, part of which crosses Ukraine, remains a key route for supplying Russian crude to Hungary and Slovakia under an exemption from European Union sanctions imposed over Moscow's war in Ukraine.
read also
Poland has no Patriot missiles left for Ukraine, Sikorski says
Poland is not in a position to provide Ukraine with U.S.-made Patriot missiles, Polish Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski told the Polish Press Agency (PAP) in an interview published on Oct. 19, as Kyiv struggles to intercept Russian missile strikes.
Sikorski said that the shortage of interceptor missiles had worsened after the attacks on Iran, and that Russia now produces more missiles.
“This is a genuine problem,” Sikorski said.
At the same time Sikorski added that other NATO countries still could transfer such resources to Ukraine, but did not specify which countries he was referring to.
For now, Sikorski said, Poland can only join in the appeals to other countries to help supply Ukraine with the much needed missiles.
The comments come as Ukraine faces renewed Russian ballistic missile attacks and increasingly severe shortages of the interceptors needed to defend against them.
Patriot systems are among Ukraine's most important defenses against Russian ballistic missiles, which are particularly difficult to intercept using other systems.
On Oct. 15, President Volodymyr Zelensky said that Polish aid helped Ukraine defend Kyiv during recent attacks, having provided ammunition used by Ukraine's anti-aircraft guns. Zelensky also hinted at other, more sensitive Polish support which would have to remain confidential; "sometimes it should remain between the two of us," he said.
On Oct. 18, Zelensky said that Washington has approved only some of the missiles purchased through the Prioritized Ukraine Requirements List (PURL) initiative, which allows NATO allies to finance the purchase of U.S.-made weapons for Ukraine, according to Bloomberg.
"The American side approved the delivery of only some of them, but not the rest. And this is not a technical issue," Zelensky said.
The Ukrainian president said the U.S. is currently supplying just 12 Patriot interceptor missiles per month, approximately one-quarter of the number provided under former President Joe Biden's administration.
read also
Russian drones strike Kyiv hospital, injure 5 across the city
Russian drones repeatedly struck Kyiv on Oct. 20, damaging a hospital in Solomyanskyi District and another medical facility in Holosiivskyi District, injuring five people, according to local authorities.
Ukrainian Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi said Russia struck the operating room of the Strazheska Institute of the National Academy of Medical Sciences in Kyiv, injuring one patient.
"This is the second time. Last year, the attack hit the fourth floor of the institute, and now it is on the sixth floor, where the operating room is located," Koretskyi said.
The medical facility in Holosiivskyi was damaged by debris from a Russian drone, Kyiv city mayor Vitali Klitschko said in the afternoon.
While Klitschko initially reported two people injured, the Kyiv City Military Administration (KMCA) later raised the total number of injured people to five.
Debris also fell on railway tracks in Solomyansyki District but did not lead to a fire, the mayor said. Several other buildings in Holosiivskyi area was also seemingly struck in the attack, according to Kyiv Independent reporters on the ground.
A large-scale fire also broke out in Kyiv's Desnianskyi District, close to the Northern Bridge, KMCA spokesperson Kateryna Pop told RBC Ukraine. Initial reports on social media that the Northern Bridge was hit were not correct.
The Kyiv City State Administration (KMDA) also said that the Northern bridge was not hit, but that traffic on the bridge may be disrupted due to inspections of the consequences of the nearby attack.
In the Obolon District, debris from a drone fell on a market, KMCA said. The consequences of the incident were still under investigation.
Following another attack in the afternoon, Klitschko said that an energy facility was hit in Shevchenkivskyi District, as emergency services were on their way.
Earlier this morning, at least three people were killed and four people injured after a Russian drone struck early morning commuter traffic in the Holosiivskyi District of Kyiv.
Ukraine's State emergency service reported the victims of Russia's drone strike, saying "The enemy is once again cynically attacking civilians. Behind each such blow are human lives, pain, and ruined destinies."
The Russian drone crashed near a gas station in the Holosiivskyi District close to the administrative border with Kyiv Oblast, Kyiv city mayor Vitali Klitschko said.
Images shared by the Kyiv Oblast Prosecutor's Office showed multiple cars ablaze at the scene of the attack near the Kyiv-Odesa highway.

articles.title: Israel unveils new space warfare unit amid Gaza genocide
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Israel unveils new space warfare unit amid Gaza genocide
Israel has established a new military Space Division to expand its surveillance and warfare capabilities, raising questions about how the technology could be used against Palestinians amid its genocide in Gaza and continuing military occupation of the West Bank.
The Israeli military announced on Monday that Brigadier General "Shin", identified only by his first initial in Hebrew, had been appointed to command the division, which will operate under the military's Planning Directorate.
The new body will oversee space-related military operations, coordinate training and intelligence, and develop capabilities for what Israel increasingly regards as a separate arena of warfare.
The military said the division was established after it concluded that "the space domain has become an active combat domain" and would play an increasingly important role in future conflicts.
Welcoming the announcement on Tuesday, Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz described the initiative as part of his ambition to transform the country into a major military space power.
"The goal set for the IDF and the defense establishment is to make Israel one of the world's leading countries in the field of space security," Katz said, describing the project as "Star Wars, made in Israel."
He said Israel wanted the "ability to monitor, defend and attack from space any target across vast areas", arguing that such capabilities would strengthen its military dominance and deter adversaries.
Satellite surveillance and the war on Gaza
However, the expansion also carries significant implications for Palestinians, who have long been subjected to Israel's extensive military surveillance and intelligence operations.
Israel already operates a network of military reconnaissance satellites whose imagery is processed by Unit 9900, a specialised military intelligence formation responsible for visual and geospatial intelligence.
The unit's work includes identifying military targets and providing intelligence to support Israeli operations, including attacks in Gaza.
Its capabilities form part of a broader Israeli intelligence infrastructure that has been deployed during the war on Gaza, where surveillance technologies and digital targeting systems have come under growing scrutiny over their role in attacks that have killed large numbers of Palestinian civilians.
Human rights organisations have raised serious concerns about Israel's use of digital intelligence and automated targeting technologies during the war, including the reliability of information used to identify suspected targets and the risks posed to civilians.
Human Rights Watch warned in 2024 that Israel's reliance on digital targeting tools in Gaza raised concerns about inaccurate data and the potential for unlawful attacks.
Although the precise responsibilities of the new Space Division remain unclear, an expansion of Israel's satellite intelligence capabilities could further strengthen the military's ability to monitor Palestinian territory, track movements and identify potential targets.
Such technology could also be used to monitor roads, border crossings, infrastructure and changes in the urban landscape across Gaza and the occupied West Bank.
There is no confirmation that the new division will directly oversee operations against Palestinians, but its establishment could consolidate capabilities already used by Israel's military intelligence services.
The distinction is significant because satellite surveillance is not merely a means of observing territory. When integrated with military intelligence and targeting systems, it can contribute directly to decisions about where and when strikes are carried out.
Expanding Israel's military reach
Israel has continued to invest heavily in reconnaissance satellites, including its Ofek series, which provide imagery for intelligence gathering and military planning.
Until now, responsibility for space-related operations, including satellite launches and ballistic missile defence, has largely rested with the Israeli Air Force, while Unit 9900 has controlled military intelligence satellites after their deployment.
The Israeli military has not clarified which responsibilities will be transferred to the new division.
According to the military, several projects involving space-based sensors and space warfare capabilities have already been approved over the past year.
A new frontier for warfare
Israel's announcement also reflects intensifying international competition over the militarisation of space, with the US, Russia, China and India developing technologies intended to protect their own satellites or disrupt those operated by adversaries.
The 1967 Outer Space Treaty prohibits the placement of nuclear weapons and other weapons of mass destruction in orbit but does not comprehensively prohibit conventional military activities in space.
Israel has also identified Iran's developing space capabilities as a potential threat.
During its conflict with Iran in March, the Israeli military claimed to have destroyed a facility in Tehran involved in military satellite development, alleging that it was also working on technology capable of attacking satellites.
The claims could not be independently verified.
Alongside the Space Division, Israel announced the establishment of a new Robotics Division under its Depth Corps, which conducts operations beyond the country's borders.

articles.title: Zelenskyy says if Trump can't stop Putin, help Ukraine do it
articles.body:
Ukraine's Zelenskyy says if Trump "cannot rein Putin in," at least clear interceptor missile shipment
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in an interview published Tuesday that if President Trump "cannot rein Putin in," he should provide long-requested interceptor missiles so Ukraine can defend itself, as the war of words between the two leaders continues to escalate.
"If you cannot rein Putin in, then give us interceptor missiles so I can protect our energy infrastructure," Zelenskyy told the Italian newspaper Corriere Della Sera, referring to Russia's autocratic President Vladimir Putin.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio said later Tuesday that Mr. Trump has been "frustrated" by what he described as false accusations that "he is doing things to deliberately harm Ukraine." He insisted that nothing had been "deliberately denied to Ukraine," but added: "It's simply, it's a balance between our obligations to other partners and frankly our own ... requirements for our own facilities as well."
The exchange came as Zelenskyy prepared to meet U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff in Norway on Tuesday, with his fellow envoy, Mr. Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner, expected to join remotely.
Zelenskyy has accused the Trump administration this week of delaying shipments of interceptor missiles to Ukraine, as well as constraining Starlink satellite data that is vital to Ukrainian forces' ability to intercept incoming Russian attack drones.
Ukraine has nearly run out of the U.S.-made Patriot air defense interceptors used to take down Russian ballistic missiles, and Zelenskyy has long pleaded for more. This week he said the U.S. was delaying delivery of Patriots already purchased by European nations for Ukraine.
Rubio, on a visit to India, said "every other country in the world" also wanted Patriots.
"I also talked to Saudi Arabia today. They'd like interceptors. Israel would like interceptors. We would like interceptors. Every country in the world would like interceptors," he said. "It's probably the most in-demand product right now in the defense field. So, when a country doesn't get interceptors from the United States, it's not because we're denying."
The meeting comes as daily Russian drone and missile attacks on Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities continue claiming civilian lives, and as relations between Kyiv and Washington appear more strained than they have been since Zelenskyy's tumultuous February 2025 meeting in the Oval Office.
The Ukrainian president said Monday that his country had suffered another night of Russian strikes, "and again there was no warning from partners." At least four people were killed in the capital in the latest attacks, Kyiv officials said Tuesday.
Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store said Finnish President Alexander Stubb would also join the talks in Oslo, with "the aim to put diplomatic efforts on a more constructive path," according to a statement from the prime minister's office.
Starshield and Patriots
Mr. Trump on Friday waived some sanctions against Russia, reducing penalties for its energy sales in a bid to ease rising U.S. gas prices caused by the ongoing war with Iran — a policy Zelenskyy says could embolden Moscow to step up its four-and-a-half-year invasion of Ukraine.
Mr. Trump has criticized Zelenskyy for saying he would resume strikes on Russian refineries in retaliation for the latest Russian onslaught.
Zelenskyy said Saturday that Ukraine was still unable to use Starshield — the military-grade version of SpaceX's Starlink satellite network — to intercept Russian drones.
The Trump administration has denied ordering Starshield restrictions. A senior Pentagon official told CBS News Monday that there had been "no change to Department of War policy regarding intelligence sharing or any capabilities we are enabling Europeans to provide to Ukraine."
In recent days, Mr. Trump has intensified his public criticism of Zelenskyy, saying in a Truth Social post that the Ukrainian leader "doesn't want to end this war, and probably never did," and telling reporters, "maybe it's time for Zelenskyy to get somebody else to negotiate."
Mr. Trump has never publicly acknowledged that Russia started the war against its neighbor, which initially began in 2014, and has at times blamed Zelenskyy for the full-scale invasion ordered by Putin on Feb. 24, 2022.
Ahead of his Tuesday meeting with Mr. Trump's envoys, Zelenskyy said he had a "substantive conversation" with Rubio the previous day in which he stressed that Starshield "needs to be restored" and ballistic missile interceptors "are needed to protect lives."
Zelenskyy told a bipartisan group of U.S. lawmakers via video call on Monday that "the Pentagon is delaying the delivery of missiles" already paid for by European countries. He said Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth hadn't signed off on the shipment.
Multiple European countries were waiting for U.S. approval to transfer their own Patriot interceptors, he added, saying he believed "some political decision has been made to slow down ... support for us."
Rubio said Tuesday that it could be accurate that a batch of interceptors purchased for Ukraine had not been delivered, but he told reporters: "I think the important takeaway for you is that there has not been some deliberate political directive to go out and harm Ukraine."
Rubio also said Mr. Trump was "frustrated because, first of all, he doesn't like to be blamed for things that aren't true, including accusations that somehow he had ordered intelligence sharing to be cut off. And that's not true. He's said that repeatedly."
"I think the president, more than anything, is responding to the insinuation that somehow he is doing things to deliberately harm Ukraine — which is not fair and not true," he added.
In his interview with the Italian newspaper, published hours earlier, Zelenskyy said Ukraine had built its relationship with Washington "on honesty, fairness, and, most importantly, transparency."
"When you lie while your people are at war, it is very painful. That is why I have always wanted to hide nothing and never lie to the President of the United States," Zelenskyy told the paper, adding: "We would like to continue having the same open, honest, and pragmatic relations with America that we have today."
"The Russians are striking. America cannot stop them," he said. "Let's believe that America really wants to, but cannot. Then, as a partner, I am willing to meet President Trump halfway: if they strike us and we cannot strike back — that is neither honest nor fair — but if this is what you need, if you cannot rein Putin in, then give us interceptor missiles so I can protect our energy infrastructure."
Trump-Xi-Putin summit on Ukraine?
U.S.-led efforts to end the nearly five-year conflict have stalled in recent months, with Washington more focused on its war with Iran.
Mr. Trump recently said he was ready to meet with Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping in China next month for talks that could include discussion of the Ukraine war.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov has confirmed that "the topic of such a hypothetical has indeed been mentioned."
Ukraine's Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said this week that any such meeting on his country's fate, without Ukraine at the table, would "only encourage Putin to continue this war."

articles.title: Russian blitz kills 7 across Ukraine as Zelenskyy head for Oslo talks
articles.body:
Russian missile and drone blitz on Ukrainian civilian areas killed at least seven people Tuesday, officials said, as President Volodymyr Zelenskyy visited Norway to secure further U.S. and European aid.
U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff, who along with Jared Kushner unsuccessfully tried to steer Russia and Ukraine toward a settlement, was also expected in Oslo, the Norwegian government said. Kushner, President Donald Trump's son-in-law, will attend the meeting by videoconference, it said.
Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store and Finnish President Alexander Stubb were scheduled to meet with Zelenskyy in the capital, Oslo.
With further U.S. support for Ukraine in doubt as relations between Zelenskyy and President Trump strained again, the Ukrainian leader said he spoke with U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who is on a trip to Asia.
The conversation followed Zelenskyy's statement to a bipartisan group of U.S. lawmakers Monday that he believes "some political decision has been made to slow down ... support for us."
Ukraine has nearly run out of U.S.-made Patriot air defense interceptors needed to stop Russia's ballistic missiles, Zelenskyy said, and he urged Washington to send more. He also said the Pentagon is delaying the delivery of missiles other countries purchased for Ukraine.
Zelenskyy also said he sought Rubio's help to ensure the United States continues to share vital intelligence with Ukraine after Kyiv received none or belated warnings about Russian missile attacks in recent days.
Zelenskyy also said speed restrictions remained in place on Kyiv's use of the military-grade version of U.S. company SpaceX's satellite internet service, hampering battlefield operations.
President Trump has also waived sanctions on Russia, a move Zelenskyy criticized as helping Russian President Vladimir Putin continue Moscow's full-scale invasion, which reaches its five-year mark in February.
Zelenskyy said he had "a substantive conversation" with Rubio.
"I am grateful for his readiness to help and his clear position," Zelenskyy said on social media.
With the Russian army stalled on the front line, Putin is trying to bomb Ukraine into submission while depriving it of vital U.S. support, Western leaders and analysts say.
European countries, worried by Russia's plans on the continent and viewing Ukraine as a bulwark against Moscow's ambitions, are trying to compensate for any decline in U.S. supplies, but some key assets are U.S.-made.
European countries and EU institutions have allocated 237 billion euros (about $266 billion) to supporting Ukraine, compared with 115 billion euros from the U.S., according to Germany's Kiel Institute, a think tank that tracks assistance to Kyiv.
EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas Tuesday questioned whether U.S. negotiators were honest brokers in peace efforts. Ukrainian officials say the Trump administration encouraged Kyiv to surrender land to Russia in return for peace.
"Although American negotiators have been trying to push Ukraine into surrender for one and a half years, why Ukraine has not surrendered on Putin's terms is because Europe has supported Ukraine," Kallas said.
"Ukraine wants peace more than anybody because it has been under bombardment for four years," she told EU lawmakers in Strasbourg, France. "The only one who does not want peace is Russia."
Russian missile and drone attacks killed four people and wounded 27 others, including children, in Kyiv region over the past day, regional police said.
Police said three people were killed and six were wounded in the Obukhiv district, where warehouses were damaged. In the Bucha district, one woman was killed and 21 people were wounded, eight of them children, and hundreds of buildings were damaged, according to police.
A Russian attack on the Kyiv-Odesa highway killed three people and injured four when two vehicles caught fire Tuesday morning, Ukraine's State Emergency Service said. Among the dead was the driver of a shuttle bus hit in the attack. The bus transports passengers from Kyiv to the National Military Memorial Cemetery.
National grid operator Ukrenergo reported power outages in 12 Ukrainian regions following the Russian attacks.
The Russian Defense Ministry said its forces conducted drone strikes on logistics centers, port infrastructure and three cargo ships in the port of Reni in Odesa region. Its forces also hit another bulk carrier at sea on its way to Odesa.
Meanwhile, air defenses intercepted 136 Ukrainian drones over multiple Russian regions overnight, the ministry said.
A fire broke out at an unspecified industrial facility in the Tambov region following the attack, Gov. Yevgeny Pervyshov said.

articles.title: Rubio insists the US isn’t trying to hurt Ukraine
articles.body:
The Ukrainian president complained about delayed air defense deliveries, the U.S. no longer warning of ballistic missile attacks and a slowdown in crucial Starlink services.
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the country had not changed its policy on sharing early warnings of Russian missile attacks with Ukraine and that the Pentagon was not deliberately withholding air defense missiles.
"There's nothing being deliberately denied to Ukraine," Rubio said during a visit to India Tuesday, calling reports that the U.S. was not giving Ukraine early warning of Russian ballistic missile attacks "outrageous."
"Everything they've been doing with Ukraine remains the same," he said of U.S. Department of Defense policy. "That has not changed. Nothing has changed."
Advertisement
Rubio's comments come as Russia escalates its attacks and Washington moves toward positions more favorable to Moscow, raising European concerns that the U.S. is not a dependable source of support for Ukraine.
Rubio was speaking shortly after the EU’s top diplomat Kaja Kallas accused Washington of trying to force Ukraine to surrender to Russia. "American negotiators have been trying to push Ukraine into surrender for already almost two years," she told the European Parliament on Tuesday morning.
On military equipment, Rubio said Ukraine's urgent appeals for more interceptors for Patriot air defense systems had to be balanced against U.S. needs — which are trying to restock thanks to the war against Iran— as well as the demands of other allies.
"I know one of the things that President Zelenskyy has been talking about is that he's been trying to buy interceptors. And I understand. So does every other country in the world," Rubio said. "I also talked to Saudi Arabia today. They'd like interceptors. Israel would like interceptors. We would like interceptors. Every country in the world would like interceptors."
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Monday accused the U.S. of holding back on sending air-defense missiles paid for by allies under the NATO-led Prioritised Ukraine Requirements List program.
“Unfortunately, the Pentagon is delaying the delivery of missiles that our partners have already paid for through the program PURL,” Zelenskyy said during a video briefing to U.S. lawmakers.
Advertisement
Zelenskyy also said that the U.S. is not always alerting Ukrainian authorities about incoming Russian ballistic missiles; such attacks have become more frequent and are killing people across Ukrainian cities.
"Unfortunately, we did not receive an early warning from our partners about the first wave of the Russian ballistic missile attack last night. And we are still facing speed restrictions on Starlink and Starshield services in various sectors of the front. The U.S. side has not provided Ukraine with any explanations regarding either of these two issues," Zelenskyy said in the Monday call.
U.S. early warning "always worked and then suddenly it malfunctioned. Nobody in Ukraine believes in this,” an official familiar with the matter told POLITICO on condition of anonymity. “Americans first said it happened because of weather conditions, then it was a software malfunction, then something else … They do not provide an official explanation.”
However, Rubio said the U.S. was looking into why Ukraine had problems with information about Russian missiles on Oct. 13 and 18, saying, "perhaps it was an internal issue in terms of them being able to take the information that was being provided and systemize it and react to it."
"I think the important takeaway for you is that there has not been some deliberate political directive to go out and harm Ukraine," Rubio said.
Ukraine is also complaining that Elon Musk's Starlink has throttled back speeds on its internet connections in Ukraine, making it difficult to intercept Russian drones.
Advertisement
Zelenskyy said Tuesday that he had raised the issues with Rubio.
"I am grateful for his willingness to help and his clear position. First, it's about interceptors against ballistic missiles, which are needed to protect lives. Second, it's about early warning of Russian ballistic missile attacks, which is vital. Third, it's about the situation around Starlink/Starshield, which needs to be restored," he said in a social media post.
The growing frictions with the U.S. come as President Donald Trump ramps up pressure on Kyiv to stop hitting Russian oil refineries and to reach a peace deal with Moscow.
“Russia, frankly, has been fine on Ukraine ... They have not been doing that much,” Trump told reporters on Monday.
Trump's special envoy Steve Witkoff traveled to Norway on Tuesday for a new round of talks on ending Russia's war against Ukraine.
U.N. Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine said that 328 civilians were killed and more than 2,000 wounded across Ukraine last month, an 85% increase from September 2025. The U.N. said that the first two weeks of October were among the deadliest for civilians in years, driven by intensified missile and drone strikes.
This story has been updated. Seb Starcevic contributed reporting.

articles.title: Zelensky’s feud with Trump endangers his plan to defend Ukraine
articles.body:
Zelensky’s feud with Trump endangers his plan to defend Ukraine
- Zelensky’s row with Trump is hurting Ukraine’s defence, with delays to Patriot missiles, possible limits on intelligence, and fears of weaker support before winter.
- NATO officials want Ukraine to calm tensions. They warn a broken US tie could force Kyiv into a painful deal with Russia and leave Europe exposed.
- Trump is putting more pressure on Kyiv while easing pressure on Moscow, including a diesel deal and softer sanctions. Zelensky will meet Steve Witkoff in Oslo for peace talks.
AI generated
KYIV – The feud between US President Donald Trump and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky is starting to compromise Ukraine’s ability to defend itself.
Strains that have lingered under the surface escalated dramatically over the past week when the Ukrainian President accused the US of throttling vital access to SpaceX’s Starshield satellite technology and delaying supplies of key Patriot interceptors to repel Russian ballistic missile strikes.
Senior NATO officials are concerned that the relationship between Zelensky and the US President could be beyond repair and may lead to Ukraine being forced into accepting a painful settlement to the war with Russia, according to a person familiar with the matter.
Zelensky is set to meet Trump’s envoy Steve Witkoff in Oslo on Oct 20 for new peace talks that would also be attended remotely by Trump’s son-in-law, Jared Kushner.
The breakdown in relations coincides with Trump fighting to salvage his majority in the Nov 3 midterm elections.
The argument risks leaving Kyiv at its most vulnerable heading into another frigid winter and with civilian casualties already surging from constant Russian attacks.
“It’s going to be a long, dark, cold winter,” said Justin Logan, director of defence and foreign policy at the Cato Institute in Washington.
“It’s almost November, their interceptor stockpiles are close to zero, the Europeans’ ability to replenish them is limited because inventories are limited.”
NATO secretary-general Mark Rutte is aware of the risks posed by the souring relationship and his main concern is to lower the temperature to make room for pragmatic solutions that ensure Ukraine has what it needs to stay in the fight, a NATO official said.
NATO officials have urged Ukraine to try and de-escalate with the US, one of the people said.
If Zelensky will not do that, then US arms supplies that are being financed mainly by the Europeans through the so-called PURL programme could eventually also be affected given Trump’s unpredictability, according to that person.
The person declined to be named because the talks are private.
The tensions between the US and Ukraine have never been so intense – or so personal – since Russia’s full-scale invasion began in 2022.
Speaking to Bloomberg News on Oct 18, Zelensky accused Trump of trying to pressure Kyiv into surrendering to Moscow.
He also said the US is delaying deliveries of crucial Patriot air defence interceptors used to defend Ukraine’s cities.
And Ukrainian officials now suspect the US is intermittently restricting intelligence sharing and early warning alerts about Russian ballistic missiles.
While Trump has denied ordering disruptions to the Starlink satellite service used by Ukraine to defend against Russian air attacks, he and his administration have openly criticised Zelensky.
They are ratcheting up pressure on Ukraine across a number of fronts, even as they lessen the leverage the US has over Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Trump said on Oct 19 that “somebody else” instead of Zelensky should negotiate on behalf of Ukraine, the day after he attacked him for the energy strikes on Russia in a lengthy post that justified his own policy towards Moscow.
“Russia frankly has been fine on Ukraine,” Trump told reporters. “They haven’t been doing much.”
Behind the scenes, Europeans are trying to help patch things up with the Trump administration, one of the people said.
But there is no plan so far for a trip to Washington, another person said, something that officials have done during previous dust-ups between Zelensky and Trump, most famously following their face-to-face confrontation in the Oval Office in February 2025.
The dispute is existential for Europe. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz warned on Oct 19 that Putin is seeking not only to defeat Ukraine, but to also undermine democracy in Europe.
“I’m trying to convince Donald Trump each time I’m meeting him that this should be in his own interest,” Merz told Bloomberg TV in an interview on Oct 19.
“A stable Europe, European continent, European Union as a partner in the world is something which is worthwhile for the Americans as well.”
Trump, who has pushed European leaders to shoulder most of the aid for Ukraine in the conflict, is ratcheting up pressure on what most analysts and even a growing number of Republican congressional allies believe is the wrong side of the war – not only by holding back offensive military support for Ukraine but also by undermining core defensive capabilities such as air defence.
The fire under the latest conflict was lit by Trump’s unilateral decision to make a deal with Russia for diesel exports earlier in October and his waiving of congressionally mandated sanctions targeting Russian energy, a series of moves that are likely to help Moscow finance its war machine.
One obvious sore point for the US President is Ukraine’s successful campaign of long-range drone strikes on Russian refineries.
The administration has tried to divert blame for rising energy prices away from the war the US started in Iran and towards the fighting between Russia and Ukraine ahead of the midterms in which Republicans are expected to lose control of at least one chamber of Congress.
Zelensky said in Oct 19’s interview that the US is delaying Patriot interceptor deliveries that Kyiv has already paid for.
The US is now supplying Ukraine with only 12 Patriot missiles a month, about a quarter of the number delivered under former president Joe Biden.
The Trump administration is also selling the missiles to Ukraine, while Biden provided them for free.
“The US inventory of Patriot missiles is very low, about 800 by our estimate,” said Mark Cancian, a former US defence budget expert now at the Center for Strategic and International Studies in Washington.
The Pentagon is worried about what is still required for operations in the Middle East, as well as in a potential conflict with China, he said.
Asked on Oct 19 if the relationship between the two administrations is fundamentally broken, Secretary of State Marco Rubio avoided a direct answer, saying that Trump’s goal is to end the war.
“He’s willing to do whatever he can to try to bring it to an end, even if that means having to nudge both sides to get there,” Rubio said. BLOOMBERG

articles.title: More ballistic missile interceptors and F-16 repairs inside Ukraine: Kyiv’s two asks to Lockheed Martin
articles.body:
Ukraine is counting on buying part of Lockheed Martin’s growing output of ballistic missile interceptors, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said. He met the US company’s team in Kyiv on 19 October and also raised servicing and repairing F-16 fighter jets inside Ukraine.
Russia keeps striking Ukraine’s power grid with ballistic missiles, and interceptor supplies fall short of that threat. Kyiv is working every route to more Patriot missiles, from US deliveries to allies’ stocks, and some have stalled. Greece, for one, has not confirmed it will hand any over, citing its own defense needs. A purchase from the missiles’ maker would add one more route.
Growing output, F-16 repairs in Ukraine
Lockheed Martin builds the PAC-3 MSE interceptors fired by Patriot air defense systems, as well as the F-16. Zelenskyy said both matter against Russian ballistic missiles and jet-powered Shahed drones. Neither area is easy right now, he added.
“We count on the opportunity to purchase some of them to protect more lives,” he wrote.
On 28 July, Zelenskyy met the company in Washington to discuss joint production. That came weeks after US President Donald Trump pledged Ukraine a license to manufacture Patriots.
A batch reportedly stuck in Washington
Meanwhile, US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has not signed off on a “significant” batch of Patriot missiles, Ukrainian officials told the Kyiv Independent. One official said allies had already paid for them. A US government official called the claims untrue, and the Pentagon did not respond. A NATO official said allied-funded deliveries, including air defense, continue. A second NATO official said some shipments could be delayed, but likely not for political reasons.
Zelenskyy told Bloomberg on 18 October that the US delivers only 12 Patriot interceptors a month. On 20 October, interceptors topped his list in a call with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio.
No purchase was announced, so new interceptors from this route remain a prospect. Meanwhile, partners’ early warnings of Russian ballistic launches have gone missing three times recently, Zelenskyy wrote. Those warnings give air defenses extra minutes to prepare.

articles.title: US investigation, Kiev’s cooperation with drug cartels: SVR statements
articles.body:
MOSCOW, October 20. /TASS/. During an investigation into the illegal activities of Mexican drug cartels, US law enforcement agencies obtained information about their cooperation with representatives of the Kiev regime, the press bureau of the Russian Foreign Intelligence Service (SVR) said in a press release.
TASS has compiled the SVR’s key statements.
Investigation
While investigating the illegal activities of Mexican drug cartels, US law enforcement agencies have obtained information about their cooperation with the Kiev regime: "According to information coming to the SVR, there is a new reason to panic in Kiev. The Ukrainian presidential office has learned that, in the course of a probe into illegal activities of Mexican drug cartels, US law enforcement agencies obtained information about their cooperation with representatives of the Zelensky regime."
The US has found that Mexican criminal groups have been sending militants to Ukraine to receive training in the assembly and combat use of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs): "The Americans have uncovered that criminal groups have, for a long time, been sending their militants to Ukraine to train them in the assembly and combat use of drones. At least 80 individuals have been identified who underwent such training within the ranks of the Ukrainian armed forces."
"Payment for this 'education' was funneled to officials close to [Vladimir] Zelensky, using funds generated by drug traffickers from the sale of illicit substances in the US."
Kiev’s concerns
Kiev recognizes that the presence of trained drone operators within drug cartels poses risks to US officers involved in combating drug trafficking along the border with Mexico: "The Ukrainian presidential office is aware that the presence of trained FPV drone operators within the ranks of drug cartels poses risks to the lives of US security officers involved in anti-drug operations along the border with Mexico."
Risks for Zelensky
Zelensky’s cooperation with drug cartels "could become yet another ‘nail in the coffin’ of his political career."
The Kiev regime’s cooperation with drug cartels, combined with attacks on Russian oil refineries, could push the US past the breaking point and lead to a refusal to assist Zelensky: "This fact comes alongside the abysmal corruption of Ukraine’s gauleiter, his offensive behavior and his disregard for Washington’s more than obvious warnings against targeting Russian oil refineries, as well as his refusal to hold an election. All this, Zelensky’s team fears, may be the last straw for the White House and force it to cancel all support to Kiev’s bloody clown."
Situation with drug cartels
The Kiev regime is stepping up its cooperation with Mexico’s largest drug cartels and facilitating the growth of drug transit from Latin America to Europe, the Foreign Intelligence Service (SVR) reported on June 29.
According to its press release, Ukrainian ports in the Odessa region have become a key transshipment hub for drug trafficking from Latin America to Europe via Poland, Moldova, and Romania.
A video posted on social media earlier allegedly showed Latin American mercenaries from Mexico, Colombia, and Panama serving in the Ukrainian armed forces in a wooded area.
One of the mercenaries shouted a slogan in support of the Jalisco New Generation Cartel and the Los Chapitos group.
According to the Milenio newspaper, which cited national intelligence documents, drug cartels are sending their fighters to Ukraine, where they participate in combat operations under the guise of volunteers to learn how to operate FPV drones.
The newspaper emphasized that members of the Sinaloa and Jalisco New Generation cartels have begun using drones with fiber-optic cables, following the example of Ukrainian servicemen.
This control technology makes the drones immune to the radio signal jammers used by the Mexican security forces.
The Mexican authorities lack the necessary technology and an effective legal framework to combat the drones that drug cartels use to attack civilians, conduct espionage, and smuggle drugs, security experts interviewed by the El Universal newspaper reported.
According to a video released on September 14 by the Donetsk People’s Republic (DPR) branch of the Russian Federal Security Service (FSB), weapons and ammunition supplied by the West to Ukraine end up in the hands of Mexican drug cartels.

articles.title: Russia has “behaved quite decently” toward Ukraine, Trump says, on the same day a Russian drone killed a one-year-old in a public park
articles.body:
US President Donald Trump said Russia had “behaved quite decently” toward Ukraine and suggested Kyiv should appoint someone else other than President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to negotiate on its behalf, even as Russian forces continue attacks across Ukraine and Washington faces questions over its support for Kyiv.
His comments came as Russia continues striking Ukrainian cities and infrastructure, with regular attacks killing civilians and damaging residential buildings and energy facilities. Russia has waged a violent war against Ukraine for more than 12 years, seeking to seize Ukrainian territory and undermine the country’s sovereignty, with widespread violence, grave human rights abuses, and killings of civilians throughout the conflict.
Speaking to reporters on 19 October, Trump said Zelenskyy should have settled the war long ago and could have secured a better deal by following his advice. He accused the Ukrainian president of not doing enough to end the war, claiming that Zelenskyy did not want to stop the fighting. Trump said he wanted the war to end and argued that Russia had “been fine” toward Ukraine, adding that Moscow “hasn’t been doing much.”
On the same day, a Russian drone struck a park near a cafe in Kharkiv Oblast, killing six people, including a 14-month-old girl killed in her stroller and an 11-year-old girl. Another 14 people were injured, including six children, according to Ukrainian officials.
Russian attacks intensify as Kyiv loses advance warnings
Russian attacks across Ukraine have intensified in recent months, with large-scale drone strikes, missile attacks, and repeated hits on energy infrastructure. The attacks have killed civilians, damaged homes and businesses, and disrupted electricity and other essential services.
Kyiv has faced repeated Russian ballistic missile attacks without the advance warnings Ukraine normally receives from international partners. The latest attack on 19 October again raised concerns about gaps in warning time, leaving residents with little time to reach shelter.
The repeated gaps have fueled concerns about Ukraine’s access to intelligence amid reports of restrictions on some US support. Ukrainian officials warned that missing launch data could weaken the country’s ability to detect incoming ballistic missiles, while Washington denied halting intelligence sharing.
Republicans push back against Trump's Russia policy
Trump's approach has drawn criticism from members of his own party, particularly over his decision to ease restrictions on Russian energy exports and his broader efforts to reach an agreement with Moscow, according to POLITICO.
Republican lawmakers have questioned whether easing pressure on Russia will help end the war or instead give the Kremlin additional revenue and leverage while its military continues attacking Ukraine. The dispute has exposed divisions within the party over how to handle Putin and the future of US support for Kyiv.
The sanctions relief followed a broader push toward economic engagement with Moscow. On 18 October, Trump's envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner had urged Zelenskyy in September to consider restoring Russian gas transit through Ukraine as part of a potential peace deal.
The proposal would revive a trade that Europe has spent years reducing because of its dependence on Russian energy. Renewed Russian energy exports could provide Moscow with additional revenue while its war against Ukraine continues.
Pressure on Kyiv as Washington considers closer ties with Moscow
Trump's comments add to tensions between Washington and Kyiv over the terms of a potential peace agreement and the level of US support for Ukraine. His suggestion that Ukraine change its negotiator raises further questions about whether his administration is willing to accept Kyiv's position in talks over its own future.
Zelenskyy has urged Washington to maintain pressure on Moscow rather than offer economic concessions. Ukrainian officials have also called for continued military assistance, particularly air defense systems, as Russia continues its campaign against Ukrainian cities and critical infrastructure.
The contrast between Trump's description of Russia's conduct and the situation on the ground remains stark. While Trump says Moscow has behaved relatively decently, Russian forces continue to launch attacks that kill civilians, damage homes, and threaten Ukraine's energy supply. The lack of advance warning before recent ballistic strikes on Kyiv has added to concerns about the consequences of reduced or unreliable US support.
