articles.title: How the battle for Hormuz is redefining power in the Gulf
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
How the battle for Hormuz is redefining power in the Gulf
As military operations between the United States and Iran seem to subside, a war of competing narratives is emerging, and opposing claims over the Strait of Hormuz are creating potentially misleading and profound consequences.
On the one hand, Iran declares that the Strait is shut down, while allowing a limited number of ships and vessels to gain safe, yet reportedly paid, passage through its territorial waters. The United States, meanwhile, continues to insist that the Strait is open and that free, unobstructed navigation is guaranteed. President Trump has gone further, declaring the Strait of Hormuz to be US territory.
Beyond these competing claims, however, lies a compelling reality. Satellite imagery and marine tracking applications undeniably show that traffic across this Strait is very limited, with navigation now operating at only a fraction of its normal level before 28 February 2026. Contrary to US claims, the severely restricted passage of commercial ships across the Strait has clearly affected the global energy market, driving a surge in oil prices.
As this narrow passage becomes congested with military fleets, tankers, and other vessels, and as international interest grows, new realities are unfolding. Reported bilateral discussions between the two coastal states bordering the Strait, Oman and Iran, have reached a critical stage, defining new routes for vessels into and out of the strait. The bilateral discussions, meticulously followed by the US and the mediators, Pakistan and Qatar, is said to introduce new realities which did not exist before the US-Israeli attacks on Iran last February.
The Maritime Security Group's open-source analysis indicates that Iran seeks a role in overseeing inbound, and possibly outbound, maritime traffic through the Strait. Tehran is reportedly demanding new arrangements concerning vessels carrying military articles that could be used in military operations against Iran. If these reports prove accurate, they would mark the beginning of a fundamental shift in how access, navigation, and security are managed in the Strait of Hormuz.
Yet, even a successful conclusion of bilateral discussions with Oman would not guarantee the reopening of the Strait. Iranian officials have stressed that reopening the Strait of Hormuz is not contingent on the successful conclusion of these talks. Rather, Tehran views US adherence to the Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) bilaterally signed with Iran as a precondition for a sustainable resumption of navigation across Hormuz. In particular, Iran is calling for swift implementation of the MOU provisions on the cessation of hostilities, the lifting of the blockade, and the easing of sanctions. This distinction is critical.
The Oman-Iran discussions may address the mechanics of navigation through the Strait, but Tehran appears to be linking the sustainability of that navigation to a much broader political and security framework.
Those familiar with Iran’s nuclear negotiations will realise the magnitude and the level of concession Tehran has made on the nuclear front. A closer look at the US-Iran Memorandum of Understanding reveals that Iran has committed itself to halting uranium enrichment, down-blending its stockpile of highly enriched uranium and imposing a moratorium on nuclear fuel cycle activities.
Amid growing speculation of a rift with Iran’s leadership, these concessions may have prompted hard-line elements, already dissatisfied with the MOU's terms, to seek to renegotiate Article 5, which addresses the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz. This is consistent to a great extent with repeated statements by Iranian officials that the “Hormuz card” is more valuable than possessing nuclear weapons; To the Iranian mindset, the strategic leverage offered by the Strait is the perfect compensation to Iran’s concession in the nuclear file.
All this suggests that the Strait of Hormuz may not return soon to pre-war conditions. For Iran, Hormuz is not simply a waterway; it is now the “guarantor”, a part of its broader strategic equation involving sovereignty, deterrence and gaining lasting leverage.
For Oman, known for its balanced relations and tradition of diplomatic mediation, this Gulf state finds itself in a peculiar yet potentially advantageous position at the forefront of emerging regional arrangements.
Other GCC states may be the greatest losers from these evolving dynamics and arrangements. Obviously, GCC states have to face the new reality that Iran is not simply a neighbour, but a “gatekeeper for Hormuz”. Given GCC economies’ heavy dependence on maritime trade and energy exports, we may soon see GCC plans for alternative routes to export/import oil and commodities. This contingency planning would profoundly affect oil prices and markets.
For the United States, a key player facing an equally difficult calculation in the region, there is a fundamental interest in keeping international navigation open across Hormuz, alongside a recognition that military pressure would backfire.
Russia, meanwhile, remains in a comfortable position, benefiting from US exemption from oil sanctions, which allows it to sell its oil to international markets. The longer the crisis in Hormuz, the greater the benefit for Russian energy exports.
For China, the calculation is different. As one of the world's largest energy consumers, Beijing has a strong interest in restoring predictable navigation through Hormuz while exploring mechanisms to evade sanctions.
Regardless of these positions, the critical question is not simply whether the Strait becomes open. It is whether regional actors can build a mechanism that keeps Hormuz open, rather than using it as an instrument of pressure.
Ayman Khalil is a Senior Researcher at the Arab Institute for Security Studies. A physicist by training and holds a Ph.D. in theoretical physics from Reading University (UK). He is the coordinator of the "Missile Capabilities Platform" and “Nuclear Forum”, the only specialized forum in the Arab world that promotes policy and public dialogue in CBRN and delivery vehicles.
Fadel Kaseb is a Senior Researcher and Lecturer at the Arab Institute for Security Studies. He possess strong academic qualification with a Diploma focused in policy and strategy from U.S Naval War college and a diploma from UK's joint staff college. He has vast experience in Defence and security studies, with a Master degree from the University of London/King's College. Brigadier retired Kaseb has specific interest in joint military operations, future and strategic foresight. Fadel Kaseb and Ayman Khalil are both coordinators of the Maritime Security Group, a Norwegian sponsored initiative.

articles.title: Trump 'open to summit with Xi and Putin'
articles.body:
US President Donald Trump said on Monday he is open to three-way arms-control talks with President Xi Jinping and Russian leader Vladimir Putin as soon as next month, raising the prospect of an unprecedented meeting.
"We would have it to talk about nuclear weapons and denuclearisation," Trump told reporters outside the White House. "If President Xi wants to have it, I'd have it. I'm sure we'd talk about other things like trade too."
The Kremlin said earlier that the Russian, Chinese and US leaders could meet at an Asia-Pacific summit in Shenzhen next month, following a Wall Street Journal report that Putin wanted the three-way talks to broker a peace deal favourable to Moscow.
The three leaders have met separately but never held formal talks together.
"I would do it, not so much for Ukraine, because Russia, frankly, has been fine on Ukraine. They haven't been doing much," Trump told reporters when asked if he would attend a meeting with Putin and Xi to discuss Ukraine.
Pressed on whether he would discuss Ukraine at any Xi-Putin summit, Trump replied that he would do "whatever I can do to end the war."
But Trump defended his recent diesel deal with Putin and decision to waive new sanctions on Moscow, which has opened a huge rift with Kyiv and prompted Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky to warn the US leader he is on the wrong side of history.
"Zelensky doesn't know what he's talking about," Trump said when asked about the Ukrainian's comments. "To be honest, I think it's time for somebody else to negotiate on behalf of Ukraine."
Moscow launched one of its broadest air assaults in months overnight, cutting power to more than half a million households and damaging energy infrastructure across Ukraine. Ten people were reported killed.
Kyiv has accused Washington of withholding vital intelligence and slowing speeds on a satellite system used to track incoming strikes.
Last week, Trump told reporters he thought a denuclearisation deal with Russia and China was possible, but that it "doesn't have to be this year." It's not clear how advanced any talks between the countries are.
Russia has the most stored nuclear warheads, followed by the United States and China, according to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute.
The Strategic Arms Reduction Treaty expired earlier this year. The New START treaty, signed in 2010, allowed a single extension, which Putin and former US President Joe Biden agreed to for five years. Any new extension would require an executive decision to voluntarily extend the limits of the treaty.
China's foreign ministry said last week that its "nuclear strength is by no means at the same level with that of the US and Russia" and that it would be "neither fair, reasonable nor realistic to ask China to join the so-called trilateral nuclear disarmament negotiations at this stage."
Trump has already agreed to attend the Apec summit in Shenzhen next month, marking his second trip to China this year and his third visit with Xi over the same period. (Agencies)
Edited by Cecil Wong

articles.title: Rubio thinks Starlink is fixed. Kyiv says it still cuts out above 161 km/h
articles.body:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on 20 October that he had spoken with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio about ballistic missile interceptors, early warning of Russian launches, and “the situation with Starlink/Starshield, which needs to be restored,” he wrote on X. He thanked Rubio for “his readiness to help and his clear position” and said they would speak again soon. A day earlier, he had told US senators how each of those supplies had stalled.
This comes as the US presses Kyiv to stop its strikes on Russian oil refineries, which Trump has blamed for high fuel prices at home, and Zelenskyy counts the Starlink slowdown among the steps he says look like an effort to push Ukraine to capitulate. Ukraine’s interceptor drones depend on the service to hunt Russia’s jet-powered Shaheds, and Kyiv says they now lose the link at speeds too low to catch them. The call appears not to have settled whether that cap is gone. If it stays, Ukrainian cities could face Russia’s drone waves this winter with one fewer means to stop them, as Russia keeps striking the grid.
On 17 October, Rubio told reporters that nobody in the US ordered Starlink slowed, that the slowdown “wasn’t deliberate,” and that “my understanding is it’s been restored.” He drew a line between the two services. Ukraine’s drones, he said, ran on commercial Starlink, while Starshield, the military version, is not available to Ukraine. Kyiv has asked for it to carry out strikes deep inside Russia, and that request is under discussion, he said.
The next day, Zelenskyy told Bloomberg that Starlink in Ukraine cuts out above 161 km/h, and Kyiv says its Starshield terminals are capped as well. His post after the call still says the service needs to be restored.
Reuters’ sources point to the White House. Washington denies it
The order to slow Starshield came from inside the White House, Reuters reported, citing two US officials and a Western official. They described it as the Starshield service for the Ukrainian military, the version Rubio says Ukraine does not have. A senior Ukrainian official told Reuters that Kyiv had been told it was a White House decision. A senior US official told the agency the president never made such a request, and the White House did not answer whether other officials had. Rubio called a report that the White House ordered Starlink slowed “categorically false.”
Missile warnings and Patriots are also in dispute
Overnight on 18–19 October, Ukraine got no partner warning before the first of two Russian ballistic waves, Air Force spokesman Yurii Ihnat said on the national telethon. That came hours after Zelenskyy said US warnings had resumed. On 19 October, Rubio pushed back against suggestions of a pause in US intelligence sharing, AFP reported.
Zelenskyy also told Bloomberg the US sends only 12 Patriot interceptors a month and has authorized only part of those “we have paid for” under PURL. Ukrainian officials told the Kyiv Independent that Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has not signed the contracts. A US government official called those claims “not true.”

articles.title: Zelensky lobbies US senators to pressure Trump – Axios
articles.body:
Zelensky lobbies US senators to pressure Trump – Axios
Vladimir Zelensky has appealed to a bipartisan group of US senators to pressure President Donald Trump into lifting alleged restrictions on US military assistance and intelligence sharing, Axios reported on Monday.
During a virtual meeting with lawmakers led by Republican Senator Thom Tillis and Democrat Richard Blumenthal on Monday, Zelensky complained about alleged disruptions to weapons deliveries, satellite communications, and early warnings of Russian missile attacks, according to a transcript obtained by Axios from Ukrainian officials.
The Ukrainian leader suggested that the Trump administration deliberately “slowed down support” to force Kiev into accepting a negotiated settlement with Moscow.
The lobbying effort comes as Trump has grown increasingly frustrated with Kiev’s refusal to halt attacks on Russian oil refineries, which he blamed for worsening the global diesel shortage and driving up fuel prices for US consumers.
The dispute escalated earlier this month after Trump struck a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to ease restrictions on Russian diesel exports and increase supplies to the global market. Kiev condemned the agreement, accusing Washington of making concessions to Moscow behind Ukraine’s back.
US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner reportedly reminded Ukrainian negotiators during talks in Miami that Washington is supplying Kiev with weapons and intelligence and that Ukraine should not pursue attacks that hurt American consumers. Ukrainian officials interpreted the remarks as a threat to suspend the assistance unless the refinery strikes stop.
The Trump administration has denied issuing any ultimatums. Secretary of State Marco Rubio has rejected claims that the administration deliberately restricted intelligence sharing or Starlink access. The Pentagon has likewise denied changing its intelligence-sharing policy.
Yet Zelensky continued to challenge the administration, telling senators that SpaceX’s Starlink and the US military’s Starshield satellite systems remain partially restricted and that Ukraine missed US early warnings about Russian ballistic missile attacks on three occasions over the past week.
He also accused Secretary of War Pete Hegseth of holding up Patriot interceptor missiles and AIM-9X missiles that NATO countries already purchased for Kiev.
The Washington Post reported that the Pentagon has yet to authorize certain transfers of Patriot missiles from third countries.
Following the meeting, Blumenthal pledged further congressional action, saying bipartisan support for Kiev remains “clear and unequivocal.”
Trump lashed out at Zelensky on Monday, accusing him of obstructing efforts to end the conflict and suggesting that someone else should negotiate on Ukraine’s behalf.
“Zelensky doesn’t know what he’s talking about,” Trump told reporters. “Maybe it’s time for Zelensky to get someone else to negotiate… We’ve given a lot to Ukraine, they’ve given nothing to us.”

articles.title: Brother Munir! The Ball Is in the US Court
articles.body:
Brother Munir! The Ball Is in the US Court
Pakistan's army chief came to Tehran to break the deadlock, but the US has repeatedly derailed mediation with fantasies like Iran's surrender
TEHRAN – Field Marshal Asim Munir, Pakistan’s army chief, arrived in Tehran on Tuesday for consultations with Iranian officials. It is General Munir's fifth visit to Tehran since the start of the US-Israeli war against Iran on February 28.
In continuation of the Pakistani government's sincere mediation, the country's army chief arrived in Tehran yesterday and held talks with senior Iranian officials. Islamabad's efforts come as Iran has always given credibility to mediators, but in recent years it is the US that has consistently neutralized those efforts and discredited them. Iran gave the four European countries the opportunity in the JCPOA to appear as international actors, but when Trump withdrew from the JCPOA in his first term, those countries failed to honor their commitments to Iran and even aligned themselves with the US policies and anti-Iran actions. After that, Iran engaged with Oman, and Muscat also sincerely tried to untie the knot between Washington and Tehran, but in the end Trump even threatened to bomb Oman, leaving observers stunned.
Pakistan's sustained efforts in the ongoing war also led to the Islamabad MoU and placed Pakistan in the position of a major international actor, but once again it was the US that destroyed it only weeks later with adventurism in the Strait of Hormuz and violation of the memorandum's provisions.
Tehran was the first country to recognize Pakistan's independence and has always had warm and close relations with Islamabad. Islamabad knows well that the Islamic Republic of Iran is a strong barrier against the sinister intentions of the Israeli regime, and if Tel Aviv's malign actions are not contained, they know no limits. Tehran and Islamabad have many common interests, and Pakistan's role and efforts in resolving the ongoing conflict are welcomed by Tehran. But has the US had, and does it have, the same view of mediators?
Pezeshkian: Iran does not trust the US
President Masoud Pezeshkian, in his meeting with the Pakistani army chief, recalling the record of US bad faith and breach of promises – attacking our country in the middle of negotiations and martyring the Supreme Leader of the Revolution, scientists and innocent schoolchildren without any legal justification – said: All the problems created in the region, from escalation of tension and conflict to disruption in the Strait of Hormuz, all stem from the warmongering nature of the US. All their claims against our country lack legitimacy, because we had proven our goodwill both with regard to negotiations and inspections in the nuclear file within the framework of international laws and regulations.
Emphasizing that the US must first show it will lift threats and sanctions so that conditions for dialogue can be met, Pezeshkian stated: You cannot increase sanctions and pressure day by day and close routes and roads to our country, and then claim you seek dialogue and negotiation. What kind of dialogue is this?
Noting that we know war benefits neither us, nor the region and the world, nor even the US, the President added: It is the US that must answer why it started the war in the first place, entangling itself and the world in problems and difficulties?
Pezeshkian noted: We have been and are ready for dialogue, but the US must first remove threats and sanctions and then we will talk, because if they are truly seeking dialogue and agreement, such behavior is completely in contradiction with their claim and is not logical.
The President, further pointing out that they imposed all these criminal acts on our country and our region under the false claim of nuclear weapons, while they martyred our Leader who had repeatedly stressed the prohibition of nuclear weapons, and drove the region into deadlock, said: They will certainly not achieve their objectives through war and will only bring destruction and damage, not only for Iran but for the entire region; something we do not want to happen.
Stressing that they must prove to our nation that this time they do not want to lie to us, Pezeshkian said: Our nation today does not trust the US and believes that if we negotiate, they will attack us again.
The President added: They constantly propagate in the media that they want to attack our country to frighten our people, while our nation has no fear of martyrdom. You, as our Muslim brothers, must make them understand that this is not how one treats Muslims. We do not want to impose our will on anyone, but we will not submit to coercion.
Field Marshal Asim Munir, in the meeting expressed pleasure at meeting Pezeshkian, presented a report on diplomatic actions and efforts to reduce tensions, and while expressing concern over a renewed outbreak of war, stressed the importance of resolving issues through diplomatic solutions and Pakistan's readiness to help settle matters in this regard.
He, while regretting the non-implementation of the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding, said: Negotiation never means weakness and acceptance of submission to the US, because the Iranian nation has repeatedly shown its dignity, authority and power to the world; rather it is an opportunity to resolve issues through a path other than war, conflict and insecurity.
Iran will not take out its uranium
General Munir also met in Tehran with the Secretary of the Supreme National Security Council. Major General Mohsen Rezaei, the Representative of the Supreme Leader and Secretary of the Supreme National Security Council, in his meeting with Asim Munir, stressing that all enriched nuclear material will remain in Iran, said: Not even an ounce of enriched nuclear material will leave Iran, and this material is a great asset and the national wealth of Iranians for use inside the country.
Major General Mohsen Rezaei stated: All the Iranian people and officials have unanimously and with one voice concluded that until confidence-building is done by the US, there will be no negotiation, and the start of this confidence-building is the fulfillment of Iran's conditions. He also stressed the fraternity of the Iranian and Pakistani nations.
Asim Munir, emphasizing the reopening of the border between Iran and Pakistan, said the Iran-Pakistan border problem has been resolved and the border has been reopened as of Tuesday.
Referring to the courageous defense and resistance of the Armed Forces of the Islamic Republic of Iran in the 40-day war, he stressed regional cooperation between the two countries without the presence of foreigners.
US threats have no effect on our decisions
The Pakistani army chief also met with Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, Speaker of Parliament, in Tehran. In the meeting, Ghalibaf, while appreciating the support of the Pakistani government and nation for Iran in conditions of war and negotiation, stressed the fraternal relations of the two countries. Asim Munir also announced the reopening of the two countries' border as of today and described border issues as temporary and technical.
Referring to Iran's deep distrust of the US and the Trump administration's violation of the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding, Ghalibaf stressed that the US can win Iran's trust only by implementing Iran's seven conditions presented in New York.
He also said that Iran is not warmongering but is fully prepared to defend the homeland and national dignity, stressing that threats and military moves cannot change the strategic decisions of the Islamic Republic, and that it is the US that must act to get out of the quagmire of war.
A deadlock that is not easy to break
General Munir's visit to Tehran took place while negotiations between Iran and the US have reached a deadlock, and Tehran's seven-day plan to reopen the Strait of Hormuz could not untie this knot either. The deep divide between the two sides' views of the balance of conflict and tension is one of the main reasons mediation efforts have failed. While the US is a short distance from the midterm elections and the Republican Party is not in good shape in the polls, Trump is trying to force Iran into submission through threats. Iran, by tightening control over the Strait of Hormuz and dealing with violating vessels seeking to pass through the strait without permission, has increased pressure on the US, and oil prices have even exceeded 110 dollars. In the latest developments, two tankers carrying a total of 4 million barrels of crude oil hit mines over the weekend; one caught fire and the other came to a halt.
The diesel deal with Putin, although it faced enormous criticism inside the US, failed to have any particular effect on prices or calm angry US consumers.
Trump has so far taken varied and sometimes contradictory positions on the midterm elections and their link to the war with Iran. He has tried to deflect the rise in fuel prices onto the Ukraine war and Biden's record by shifting blame. Meanwhile, he has at one point spoken of the insignificance of these elections for his Iran policy and even said the elections and their outcome do not matter to him at all, but in practice he behaves differently. From the 5,000-dollar promise to every US adult and personal appearances at campaign rallies in various states, telling people to imagine they are going to the ballot box to vote for him, all show how vital this election is for him.
The US President recently said he would not start a new round of confrontation with Iran until after the elections, but evidence does not necessarily confirm this claim. The secret trip of Pete Hegseth, the US Secretary of War, to Israel and his consultations with Benjamin Netanyahu, the Israeli Prime Minister, held with the participation of officials from the UAE, has increased doubts about the future plans of the US and Israel.
Iran is ready for the next round of war
 
In Iran too, senior military officials speak of full readiness for a new round of war. Sardar Hossein Mohebbi, in his recent interview with the Tehran Times, did not rule out the possibility of a new US attack aimed at manufacturing an achievement on the eve of the elections, stressing that such an attack would bring no achievement for the US and that even if limited, Iran's response would be very severe and would confront the world with a serious energy crisis.
The IRGC spokesman, in other remarks, named data cables on the floor of the Persian Gulf as one of the possible targets in a new round of war – something that Mohsen Rezaei, the Secretary of the Supreme National Security Council, had also pointed to before him.
Major General Abdollahi, Chief of the General Staff of the Iranian Armed Forces, also said: Our enemies possess modern and new equipment, and we must, when necessary, respond to the enemy with different methods and asymmetric equipment, as happened in the two recent wars.
In the event of any renewed miscalculation by the enemy, we will neutralize the effect of the enemy's expensive and advanced equipment with a wide range of cheap but effective equipment, and this will be painful, worrying and costly for the enemy.
It seems Trump is seeking even a temporary achievement to pass easily and triumphantly through the upcoming elections, but whether he loses or wins this election, it is unlikely to fundamentally affect his strategy toward the war with Iran. Trump has openly and fully endorsed Netanyahu in the Israeli elections, and Netanyahu has explicitly stated that his goal is the destruction of Iran. The Israeli Prime Minister spoke by phone with Trump on Monday and, by his own account, stressed in it the need to achieve this goal. In such circumstances, there is no doubt about the real intentions of the Donald-and-Bibi duo toward Tehran, and this very fact undermines any mediation and proposal.
Trump is not after a deal
While some unofficial sources in the region have said Pakistan and Qatar have prepared a proposal covering part of both sides' demands that could be agreed by Tehran and Washington, evidence shows that from Tehran's perspective, Trump is merely seeking to pass through the difficult strait of the midterm elections, not to end an unjustified and costly war whose declared objectives have changed repeatedly.
Tehran has no doubt about Islamabad's sincerity in resolving the current situation, but the point is that the ball is in Washington's court, not Tehran's. Until the US government abandons the illusion of forcing Iran to surrender and imposing its unilateral conditions – whether through negotiation or military aggression – this conflict and tension will not end.
It is worth noting that concurrent with General Munir's presence in Tehran, Mohammad Ishaq Dar, Pakistan's Foreign Minister, announced at the Shanghai Cooperation Organization meeting in Tajikistan that Islamabad continues to work to reduce tensions and mediate between Tehran and Washington.
Stressing that dialogue and diplomacy are the most effective way to resolve regional disputes, he said: "Pakistan will continue to support dialogue and the peaceful settlement of disputes to achieve lasting peace and stability."

articles.title: “Give Us Interceptor Missiles”: Zelenskyy Backs Energy Ceasefire With Russia if US Helps Ukraine
articles.body:

“Give Us Interceptor Missiles”: Zelenskyy Backs Energy Ceasefire With Russia if US Helps Ukraine
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has reaffirmed Ukraine’s commitment to maintaining open and transparent relations with the United States, while expressing support for a mutual energy ceasefire with Russia, provided Washington supplies sufficient interceptor missiles to protect Ukrainian energy infrastructure.
In an interview with Corriere della Sera on October 20, Zelenskyy emphasized the importance of honesty and cooperation in Ukraine’s relationship with the United States, according to remarks published on his official Telegram channel.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
“I have always wanted to hide nothing and never lie to the President of the United States. In any case, we have more in common than America does with Russia. Most people in Ukraine and the United States understand this. We would like to continue having the same open, honest, and pragmatic relations with America that we have today,” Zelenskyy said.
The Ukrainian president noted that Kyiv and Washington have maintained strong strategic ties, which have developed particularly actively since the beginning of Russia’s full-scale invasion.
He also expressed gratitude for US assistance, stressing that Ukraine has consistently sought to build its relationship with Washington on honesty, fairness, and transparency.
Addressing the possibility of an energy ceasefire with Russia, Zelenskyy reiterated that Ukraine supports a reciprocal agreement under which both sides would refrain from targeting each other’s energy infrastructure.
However, he stressed that Ukraine must retain the ability to defend itself against Russian attacks, arguing that any restrictions on Ukrainian retaliatory strikes should be accompanied by additional air defense assistance from the United States.
“Our position is very simple. We support a mutual energy ceasefire. If we are talking about not responding against Russian energy facilities after they strike our gas, electricity, oil—everything. The Russians strike. America cannot stop them. Let us believe that America really wants to, but cannot,” Zelenskyy said.
The Ukrainian president added that he was prepared to accommodate US President Donald Trump’s position on limiting attacks against energy infrastructure, but insisted that Ukraine should not be left defenseless.
“Then, as a partner, I am willing to meet President Trump halfway: if they strike us and we cannot respond, that is neither honest nor fair. But if that is what you need, and you cannot restrain Putin, then give us interceptor missiles so I can protect our energy infrastructure. If you could not stop Putin, you helped Ukraine instead,” he stated.
Zelenskyy’s remarks come amid continued Russian strikes on Ukraine’s energy system, highlighting the importance of additional air defense capabilities as Kyiv seeks to protect critical infrastructure.
On October 14, Russian forces struck all three of Kyiv’s combined heat and power plants during a large-scale missile attack that also targeted key energy facilities in Kharkiv and the surrounding region, according to Ukrainian Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi.
Koretskyi said Russian ballistic missiles specifically targeted energy infrastructure in Kyiv, Kharkiv, and the Kharkiv region. Additional strikes hit critical facilities in the Kyiv region responsible for supplying electricity to the capital and central parts of Ukraine.
At the same time, Ukraine’s efforts to strengthen its air defenses have reportedly faced delays in the delivery of US-made interceptor missiles.
According to The Kyiv Independent on October 19, citing a senior Ukrainian official and two military officials familiar with the matter, US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has yet to authorize a substantial shipment of Patriot interceptor missiles to Ukraine.
The reported delay has raised concerns among Ukrainian officials that Washington may be withholding the weapons to exert political pressure on Kyiv, despite Ukraine’s continued reliance on Patriot systems to defend against Russian ballistic missile attacks.

U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio told Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy during a phone call on Tuesday, October 20, that U.S. President Donald Trump hasn't issued any kind of order to harm Ukraine. Axios reported this, UNN writes.

The conversation, according to the publication, was an attempt to prevent further escalation of the "crisis" between the United States and Ukraine, as well as to refute Ukraine's accusations that Trump is trying to force Zelenskyy to make concessions to russia.

articles.title: North Korea Wants Security Talks With the US, Not Nuclear Talks
articles.body:
Since the start of his second administration, U.S. President Donald Trump has repeatedly proposed renewed talks with North Korea. Pyongyang has said that relations could improve if Washington respected its nuclear status and abandoned what it calls its “hostile policy.” But what would North Korea be willing to talk about if discussions resumed?
Pyongyang increasingly seeks talks on its security concerns, particularly U.S. military policy and the regional security environment, while treating its own possession of nuclear weapons as non-negotiable. It may even demand a halt to U.S. military exercises with its allies as a precondition for talks.
What Pyongyang Learned From Hanoi
The failure of the 2019 North Korea-Trump summit in Hanoi may have prompted Pyongyang to reassess its negotiating strategy and strengthen its commitment to retaining nuclear weapons. At the summit, North Korea sought partial relief from United Nations sanctions in exchange for dismantling its Yongbyon nuclear facilities. Washington, however, sought denuclearization measures extending beyond Yongbyon in exchange for a broader package of economic benefits. The summit ended without an agreement.
Why did North Korea not accept Washington’s “big deal”? Shortly after the summit collapsed, North Korean Foreign Minister Ri Yong Ho explained that security guarantees mattered more to Pyongyang than sanctions relief. North Korea had nevertheless proposed partial sanctions relief in return for dismantling Yongbyon because it believed Washington would find it difficult to take military measures at the time.
North Korea may have recognized the limits of what the United States could offer in terms of security guarantees. U.S. military strategy in Northeast Asia is not solely a response to the North Korean threat. It also reflects Washington’s alliance commitments to South Korea and Japan and its broader strategic competition with China. Even if North Korea gave up all its nuclear weapons, Washington might not be able to offer the security guarantees Pyongyang wants, given its regional interests and alliance commitments. From this perspective, North Korea’s attempt in Hanoi to exchange partial denuclearization for partial sanctions relief may have been a realistic approach. The failure in Hanoi appears to have convinced Pyongyang that giving up its nuclear weapons would not secure the guarantees it sought. After Hanoi, North Korea reinforced its commitment to retaining nuclear weapons through legislation and constitutional changes. In September 2022, it adopted a new law on nuclear forces policy. Kim Jong Un declared that North Korea’s status as a nuclear weapon state was irreversible and ruled out further negotiations on giving up its nuclear weapons or on denuclearization.
North Korea did not begin identifying itself as a nuclear weapon state in 2022. It had already codified that status in a 2013 law “consolidating the position of nuclear weapons state for self-defense.” Article 9 of that law, however, expressed support for international nuclear disarmament efforts. The omission of that provision from the 2022 law was therefore significant.
The 2022 law not only entrenched nuclear possession as a permanent foundation of national strategy but also called for qualitative and quantitative improvements in nuclear forces in response to external threats and changes in the international nuclear balance. In this context, a freeze on nuclear weapons production or a reduction in its nuclear arsenal could conflict with this policy if North Korea’s security environment remained unchanged.
Setting the Terms for Renewed Talks
North Korea’s recent statements on relations with Washington indicate that it expects changes in U.S. policy before talks resume, while treating its nuclear possession as non-negotiable.
In October 2025, Trump publicly expressed his desire to meet Kim Jong Un again during his trip to Asia. That didn’t eventuate, but Trump is reportedly looking at the possibility of a meeting with Kim during his next trip to Asia in November 2026.
At the Ninth Workers’ Party Congress in February 2026, Kim Jong Un stated that relations with the United States could improve if Washington respected North Korea’s status as a nuclear weapon state and abandoned its hostile policy. He thus linked improved relations to a change in Washington’s attitude toward a nuclear-armed North Korea and its policy toward Pyongyang.
In August, Trump again expressed interest in meeting Kim and ordered a reduction in South Korea-U.S. military exercises. Kim Yo Jong, Kim Jong Un’s sister and an authoritative voice for the regime, dismissed the move as insufficient. She argued that holding the exercises at all demonstrated Washington’s hostility. Kim Yo Jong’s response suggested that Pyongyang wanted the exercises halted altogether, rather than merely scaled back, before agreeing to talks. In the same statement, she also criticized South Korea’s push to acquire nuclear-powered submarines.
In September, Foreign Minister Choe Son Hui reaffirmed that North Korea’s nuclear status was irreversible. She rejected the coexistence of confrontation and dialogue in relations with North Korea and argued that a geopolitical realignment centered on a nuclear-armed North Korea was inevitable. Her statement reinforced the message that Washington could not maintain policies Pyongyang regarded as hostile and expect dialogue to follow.
North Korea has long sought security guarantees and an end to Washington’s hostile policy. The difference now is that Pyongyang treats its nuclear possession as non-negotiable and expects changes in U.S. attitudes and military policy before talks resume. A reduction in South Korea-U.S. military exercises alone appears insufficient to meet its demands. Its criticism of South Korea’s nuclear-powered submarine plans also suggests concern about potential U.S. support for such capabilities.
This departs from the Singapore agreement, which paired a commitment to denuclearization with improved relations and the establishment of a peace regime. Pyongyang now seeks U.S. policy changes as the starting point for diplomacy, rather than as part of a bargain over giving up its nuclear weapons.
North Korea’s strategy notwithstanding, its ability to change U.S. policy is not guaranteed. Despite Trump’s efforts to engage Pyongyang, the United States, South Korea, and Japan continue to reaffirm the goal of North Korea’s denuclearization, while Washington maintains its defense commitments to its allies.
Pyongyang may see no need to rush into talks. It continues to build up its nuclear forces, citing security threats, while strengthening ties with its partners.
In September 2026, the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) reported signs of a new uranium enrichment facility at Yongbyon and indications of expanded operations at Kangson. North Korea has also recently increased the frequency of its missile tests. Meanwhile, expanding military cooperation with Russia and improving relations with China are giving Pyongyang greater room to resist international pressure, including sanctions. Both countries oppose further sanctions on North Korea and have become quieter on its denuclearization.
North Korea may believe that time is on its side: As its nuclear capabilities grow and its diplomatic options expand, Washington may eventually have no choice but to enter talks on the basis that North Korea will retain its nuclear weapons.
How the United States Should Respond
Washington’s first task is to clarify the conditions under which North Korea is willing to negotiate and the agenda it is prepared to discuss. Some experts argue that a nuclear freeze or reductions should serve as interim goals if complete denuclearization cannot be achieved in the short term. This may be a realistic alternative for the United States, but Washington should not assume that Pyongyang will accept it as a topic for negotiation. North Korea may instead demand that negotiations focus on regional security issues or insist on changes in U.S. policy before agreeing to talks.
To clarify these issues, working-level meetings should precede any new North Korea-U.S. summit. Washington must coordinate closely with Seoul and Tokyo before negotiating measures that affect their security. If Pyongyang raises concerns about U.S. military activities on the Korean Peninsula, Washington should assess whether its demands can be addressed through reciprocal military measures.
Discussing regional security does not necessarily mean recognizing North Korea as a nuclear-weapon state or weakening allied military readiness. With South Korea’s agreement, for example, the United States could consider adjusting the scale or format of joint exercises in exchange for limits on North Korean exercises in specific areas, with arrangements for both sides to verify compliance. Once military crisis-management measures are in place and the security environment improves, Washington could argue that Pyongyang should move toward a nuclear freeze or reductions.
The United States must also challenge North Korea’s calculation that time is on its side. Maintaining existing sanctions and deterrence alone is unlikely to change Pyongyang’s strategic judgment. The United States should make clear that North Korea’s continued nuclear buildup could lead South Korea and Japan to strengthen their military capabilities and fuel calls in both countries for nuclear weapons of their own. An offer to discuss regional security should accompany that message. The aim should be to create incentives for diplomacy without triggering another arms race.
Washington should use security talks to pursue reciprocal military measures and build a path toward limits on North Korea’s nuclear capabilities. Knowing what each side is willing to offer before the next summit would improve the chances of reaching an agreement.

articles.title: Round-the-clock Russian terror: how much longer will the enemy be able to attack Ukraine continuously
articles.body:
Round-the-clock Russian terror: how much longer will the enemy be able to attack Ukraine continuously
Kyiv • UNN
Russia has intensified its drone attacks, seeking to exhaust air defenses and pressure Ukraine. Stronger defense and strikes against Russia's military-industrial complex could reduce the attacks.
Russia continues its massive drone attacks on Ukraine and is attempting to cover as large an area as possible with its strikes. Military expert Oleh Zhdanov told a UNN journalist more about why the Russian Federation is relying on massive air attacks, how they are connected to political pressure on Ukraine, and what could force Russia to reduce the intensity of its strikes.
Details
Russian drone attacks are taking place virtually around the clock, but the nature of the air strikes changed at the end of October. According to the military expert, whereas reactive drones predominated earlier, Russia is now once again actively using conventional attack drones. In addition, the enemy is attempting to simultaneously cover as much of Ukrainian territory as possible with its attacks.
It is very strange that now "our old song is starting again—we are starting it all over again." In the sense that they are now going to attack 24/7. And what have they been doing all this time? Even now, if you look out the window, air raid alerts are in effect 24/7 across most of Ukraine. And we made it through the whole of September like that
Russia plans to increase drone production: Politico learned the details21.09.26, 10:29 • 5874 views
At the same time, Oleh Zhdanov noted that at the end of September, short intervals began to appear between drone raids. In particular, in Kyiv and other cities, there was sometimes approximately an hour between successive attacks, but at the end of October, Russia once again intensified its attacks.
The difference at the end of October is that they began trying to cover all of Ukraine. They have returned again: whereas in September they were mostly reactive, now they have once again added conventional "Shaheds" and "Geran-2" drones. And their number is greater—more than half of the drones in these continuous raids at present
Ballistic missiles also remain a separate threat; their launches, Oleh Zhdanov emphasizes, are more difficult to predict. He explains that recently Russia has used them at intervals of approximately once every 7–10 days. Moreover, the intensity of such strikes may vary, so Ukraine must also be prepared for combined attacks.
Will Russia have enough resources for continuous attacks
The expert notes that Russia is using the means of destruction at its disposal, while the scale of drone use depends, in particular, on production capabilities.
They can provide a large number of drones—and they do. Note that in September they were stockpiling conventional "Geran-2" drones. In fact, they used very few of them for a month, and then in the first ten days of October they carried out two powerful strikes, when the number of conventional drones exceeded 500 units. And now they are launching them within the limits produced by their enterprises
At the same time, Oleh Zhdanov believes that Russia has limited capacity to accumulate large stockpiles of weapons, so it is forced to constantly replenish the resources it has used. However, this does not mean that the intensity of the attacks will necessarily decrease in the near future.
They are essentially operating straight from the production line; there are very few stockpiles at present. And I say again, we have two options: the first is to destroy their production facilities, but we cannot reach them, plus they have now begun burying the same "Geran" drones in the ground. So the second option is to build an air defense system in a new, modern sense, rather than according to the old approaches of the Soviet Union or the Second World War
Why Russia is relying on drones
Massive drone attacks allow Russia to exhaust Ukrainian air defenses over a prolonged period and create a constant threat to the civilian population and infrastructure. In the expert's view, the Kremlin seeks to use these strikes as an instrument of pressure on Ukrainians in order to secure concessions on its own terms.
The objective is one and only one—to break public opinion so that people agree to capitulate on the terms of the Russian Federation. And now, by the way, negotiations are underway in Norway, and it is the same old song: "Surrender, and everything will be fine for you. If you do not surrender to us, we will continue the shelling." That's all
The expert also links the intensity of Russian attacks, in particular, to the upcoming midterm elections in the United States and negotiations on ending the war, in order to increase pressure on Ukraine precisely during periods of important international events.
Absolutely. putin always ties powerful shelling of Ukraine and massive combined strikes to political events. Today, the midterm elections in the United States are at the top of our agenda. And in fact, in my view, both Trump and putin have simultaneously gone all in. They are applying pressure in every way they can, - with all available forces and means
What could force Russia to reduce the number of strikes
The expert identifies strengthening Ukraine’s air defense as one of the key areas for countering Russian attacks. In his opinion, it is necessary to improve the ability to intercept targets at short and medium ranges, as well as to develop weapons capable of destroying threats before they are used. In addition, strikes against Russia’s military-industrial enterprises also play an important role.
Sanctions are a long song. And the most effective sanctions are our missiles and our drones. Unfortunately, our strikes against military-industrial complex enterprises are not as powerful as one would like, because even a drone carrying 100 kilograms of explosives is not a missile carrying 300 or 500 kilograms of explosives
Oleh Zhdanov also drew attention to the importance of ballistic weapons, which, according to him, could enhance Ukraine’s ability to strike Russian launchers and other military targets. At the same time, the effectiveness of countermeasures depends not only on the availability of such weapons, but also on the ability to detect targets in a timely manner and strike them. The expert believes that the development of indigenous missile technologies could become one of the factors deterring Russian attacks.
If we had ballistic missiles, we would take out the launchers or at least drive them away from the border so that they could not reach our territory. There is very little time to hit a launcher at its launch position or in the loading area. That is why Russia is very afraid of Ukraine acquiring ballistic weapons

articles.title: Are newsrooms burying Iranian efforts to influence midterms? - opinion
articles.body:
Who could ignore the constant drumbeat of newscasters, politicians, and voters lamenting the cost of gas at the pump?
A month before the war began in February 2026, a gallon of regular gasoline cost about $2.80, according to the US Energy Information Administration. By October, the price had climbed above $4.30, though it briefly dipped to about $3.70 in July.
With the midterm elections drawing near, voters have made fuel costs a top concern, blaming US President Donald Trump for the war’s effect on prices. Commentators, including Ali Velshi and Christiane Amanpour, have branded the conflict Trump’s “war of choice” while discussing its costs.
But the newsrooms that have scrutinized the war’s costs have largely overlooked a consequential account of Iran’s intentions that Reuters published on October 14, citing two senior Iranian officials: Tehran has been targeting ships to keep oil prices high to influence the US midterms.
In September, Trump accused Iran of trying to influence the election.
“They can’t hold out any longer. They’re desperate to try and affect the election so that we can get a nice, weak group of people in there and leave them alone and let them have their nuclear weapons,” he told reporters.
Politico, CNN, and The Washington Post reported his remarks. However, these same outlets did not include the Iranian officials’ remarks, leaving readers to assume that the comments were simply political fodder.
Later in September, Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps spokesperson Gen. Hossein Mohebbi read from what he called a “letter to the American people” at a press conference in Tehran.
In subsequent remarks to the Associated Press, Mohebbi urged Americans to reconsider their leadership and protest Trump’s policies, denouncing what he called their government’s warmongering.
Around October 14, Iranian attacks sank two ships near the Strait of Hormuz. CNN, The Washington Post, The Wall Street Journal, The New York Times, and Fox News covered the sinkings and the broader surge in attacks. The Times reported that attackers had struck more ships in the preceding week than in the entire month of September.
That same day, Reuters reported a piece of the story vital to Americans weighing the war and gas prices.
The two senior Iranian officials told Reuters that Iran was “deploying new tactics to target ships” sailing through the Strait as it sought to keep oil prices high and influence the midterm vote.
One official said Iran had changed the type and pace of its attacks to frustrate US and allied efforts to lower global oil prices.
According to Reuters, Iran’s senior leadership approved the strategy and coordinated it across the country’s ruling system. Tehran aimed to expand its operations beyond the strait into the Gulf of Oman and farther.
The second official said Tehran intended to prevent Trump from lowering oil prices before the elections.
CNN reported an analyst’s assessment of the strategy but left out the officials’ account. Matt Smith, an analyst at maritime-tracking firm Kpler, said, “It appears Iran is attempting to keep oil prices high ahead of the midterm elections, and the best way to do this has been to increase attacks – both from themselves and via the Houthis.”
A CNN broadcast likewise told viewers that analysts saw the attacks as part of Tehran’s effort to keep oil prices high through the elections.
However, an analyst’s speculative assessment does not hold the same weight as Iranian officials confirming that the regime is using the strategy, which CNN did not include.
Major newsrooms regularly publish Reuters reporting, including accounts that draw on unnamed officials.
Yet the coverage from CNN, The Washington Post, MS NOW, and The New York Times did not put these officials’ statements before their audiences while covering the attacks, gas prices, or foreign election influence.
Fox News buried the Reuters report solely within its live blog. Editors chose which parts of the story their audiences would see.
Sabotaging Americans from afar
Other developments made the question of Iranian influence more pressing.
On October 14, X/Twitter’s Global Government Affairs account said the platform had identified and suspended more than 13,000 accounts across three suspected foreign influence operations linked to Iran, Russia, and China.
According to X, the networks used inauthentic accounts to post and amplify content about US politics and targeted candidates and public figures across the political spectrum.
The New York Times reported the announcement on October 16, but its article focused on Russia and did not examine Iran’s role.
Still, unlike digital disinformation campaigns, Tehran’s strategy is not just an effort to change minds online; it is actively economically sabotaging ordinary Americans.
Earlier in October, The Washington Post reported that a National Intelligence Council assessment identified Iranian activity, though “not on the scale of Russia or China.”
The article also noted that US intelligence considered direct interference with voting machines or vote counts unlikely. But Iran does not need to touch a ballot to try to influence an election. Iran’s reported strategy uses force to raise costs for ordinary people to sway their votes.
News outlets have devoted significant attention to Trump’s responsibility for the war and to the financial pain Americans feel at the pump. Reuters’ account belongs in that coverage.
If senior Iranian officials told the wire service that Tehran was targeting shipping to sustain high oil prices and influence the midterms, Americans deserve to know.
Newsrooms that routinely rely on Reuters, including its interviews with unnamed officials, should not leave that account out of a story they already consider important.
An admission like this carries immense weight – a foreign adversary openly attempting to manipulate fuel markets to sway voters strikes at the very heart of American democracy.
The omission raises serious questions about the editorial priorities of newsrooms and whether political agendas shaped their coverage.
It also risks helping a foreign adversary influence an American election by denying voters information they deserve.
The writer is a US media researcher at the Committee for Accuracy in Middle East Reporting and Analysis (CAMERA) in Israel. She was previously a Breaking News desk manager at The Jerusalem Post.

articles.title: Hegseth and Netanyahu hold secret talks – Axios
articles.body:
Hegseth and Netanyahu hold secret talks – Axios
US Secretary of War Pete Hegseth has made an unannounced visit to Israel for talks with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu just days before the country’s parliamentary elections, according to Axios.
The reported meeting comes as Washington and Israel discuss potentially resuming major military operations against Iran, while indirect negotiations continue over the war they launched in February. Israel, a major recipient of American military funding and weapons, has justified its offensives on security grounds, even as the conflict has spread across the region, disrupted shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, and driven up global energy prices.
Hegseth met Netanyahu on Monday at Ovda Air Base in southern Israel, where US fighter jets and refueling aircraft are stationed, Axios reported on Tuesday, citing sources familiar with the visit. The Pentagon chief also met American troops deployed at the facility.
The talks were held behind closed doors, with neither side publicly disclosing what was discussed, the outlet said. The Pentagon declined to comment on the meeting, while Hegseth acknowledged visiting US troops operating under Central Command.
The surprise visit followed US President Donald Trump’s public endorsement of Netanyahu ahead of the October 27 parliamentary elections – Israel’s first since the Hamas-led October 7, 2023 attacks and the subsequent devastating Israeli military campaign in Gaza. On Sunday, the US president hailed Netanyahu as a “Great Warrior Prime Minister” and offered him his “Complete and Total Endorsement.”
“BIBI NETANYAHU WILL NEVER LET YOU DOWN!” Trump declared on Truth Social, praising the Israeli leader’s role in the US-Israeli war against Iran.
Netanyahu has ruled Israel for more than 18 years across several terms, longer than any other prime minister in the country’s history. He now faces a fierce battle to stay in power, with opponents blaming him for the catastrophic security failures of the October 7 attack and accusing him of prolonging the devastating war in Gaza to preserve his political survival. Polls suggest his right-wing coalition could lose its parliamentary majority.
Hegseth’s trip also reportedly comes as Washington and West Jerusalem discuss the possibility of unleashing another major military campaign against Iran. Trump has raised the prospect of renewed strikes after the US midterm elections in November.
Netanyahu has meanwhile made clear that Israel is prepared to attack Iran without waiting for Washington’s approval or participation.
“If we need to act alone, we will act alone,” he declared on Sunday, outlining a security doctrine centered on preemptive military action.
Netanyahu has also called for the overthrow of Iran’s government, claiming Tehran would continue to rebuild its military and nuclear capabilities as long as its current leadership remains in power. Iran has repeatedly denied seeking nuclear weapons, insisting its nuclear program is peaceful.

articles.title: Rubio said that the United States must weigh Ukraine’s need for air defense missiles against that of others
articles.body:
Rubio said that the United States must weigh Ukraine’s need for air defense missiles against that of others
Kyiv • UNN
The United States must balance the requests of Ukraine, other allies, and its own needs for interceptor missiles. Rubio assured that supplies are being replenished.
The United States must balance Ukraine’s urgent requests for air-defense missiles with similar demands from other allies, as well as the needs of its own military. U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said this on Tuesday, October 20, UNN reports, citing Bloomberg.
Details
The United States is responding to many such requests and cannot meet them all, Rubio told reporters in Mumbai on Tuesday.
"I know that one of the things President Zelenskyy has talked about is that he has been trying to purchase interceptor missiles, and I understand that. So is every other country in the world," the U.S. secretary of state said.
He named Saudi Arabia and Israel among the other countries seeking to obtain these weapons and added: "We also have our own needs."
Rubio said he had spoken for about 45 minutes earlier on Tuesday with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who, the publication writes, "is embroiled in an escalating dispute with Donald Trump." The U.S. president repeated his criticism on Monday following reports, according to the publication, from officials in Kyiv about restrictions on intelligence sharing.
Rubio said that the U.S. president had never ordered such changes and was upset by reports that were "inaccurate." Referring to reports that some Russian missiles had managed to strike Ukraine without the warnings they usually receive through U.S. intelligence, he said this could have resulted from a technical problem rather than a U.S. directive, the publication writes.
The U.S. secretary of state also sought to play down concerns expressed by some analysts that the United States currently has limited weapons stocks due to the cumulative effect of the war with Iran and the dispatch of a significant amount of weapons to Ukraine earlier, the publication notes.
"I think we are very satisfied with our stocks of various munitions, including interceptors," he said, adding that production had been increased.
"But it takes time to build up these stocks," Rubio emphasized.

articles.title: A diesel tank burns at Transneft’s Druzhba hub as Ukraine keeps striking Russian energy despite Trump’s pressure
articles.body:
Drones attacked an oil and fuel pumping station of Russia’s Druzhba pipeline system in Tambov Oblast overnight on 20 October, setting a diesel tank on fire, Ukrainian monitoring channel Exilenova+ reported, citing locals. Druzhba, Russian for “friendship,” is a Soviet-era oil pipeline, about 4,000 km long, that carries Russian crude west to Europe, including through a branch that crosses Ukraine. The struck station is on its Russian section. Tambov Oblast Governor Yevgeny Pervyshov confirmed a fire at an unnamed enterprise in Michurinsk district after what he called a Ukrainian drone attack. The station lies about 400 km from the front line.
Ukraine has spent months striking the refineries, terminals, and pipelines that fund Russia’s war, and its Defense Ministry says the strikes have knocked out more than half of Russia’s refining capacity. Washington wants them stopped. US officials reportedly tied intelligence sharing to a halt in refinery strikes, and US President Donald Trump called their resumption “a disgrace.”
Hours of attack before dawn
Russia’s regional alert system declared a drone threat at 03:38, Ukrainian military outlet Militarnyi reported. By 06:25, Exilenova+ said the Nikolskoye station was under attack, after Michurinsk had been under attack for several hours.
Pervyshov said four Ukrainian drones were shot down over the region and no one was hurt. He did not name the site.
Ukraine has not commented. The General Staff’s 20 October list of overnight strikes does not mention Tambov Oblast.
A Druzhba fuel hub hit before
The Nikolskoye station belongs to Transneft, Russia’s state pipeline operator. It stores and pumps crude oil and refined fuels, including diesel, gasoline, and jet fuel. The complex has three tank farms and two pumping stations, and it can move up to 300,000 tonnes a day, according to Current Time.
Ukrainian drones hit a station of the same hub in August 2025, and Ukraine’s General Staff said then that pumping on the pipeline had stopped completely.
Strikes resume despite US pressure
Ukraine paused refinery strikes for three days after Trump announced an “energy ceasefire” on 11 October, while Russia fired 39 ballistic missiles at Ukraine’s grid. Since Kyiv resumed the strikes, drones have also hit an oil terminal and a fuel depot in St. Petersburg.
Kyiv reads other US moves as pressure too, from missed warnings of Russian ballistic launches to a Starlink cap that slows Ukrainian drones. President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy told US senators he had offered a 30-day halt on refinery strikes in exchange for Patriot interceptors, but Trump’s envoys showed no openness.

articles.title: Without US intelligence, Ukraine cannot counter ballistic missiles — lawmaker
articles.body:
MOSCOW, October 20. /TASS/. Without US intelligence, Ukraine is unable to counter ballistic missiles, and Kiev’s European allies will not be able to make up for American aid, member of Ukraine’s Verkhovna Rada (parliament) Alexey Goncharenko (listed in Russia as extremist and terrorist) said.
"Last night I heard ballistic missiles coming in <...> all night long. And we heard that there were only incoming missiles, but no outgoing ones (referring to the operation of Ukrainian air defense systems). We have nothing to shoot down ballistic missiles with without the Americans. What’s more, as it turns out, without the Americans, we don’t even know when they take off or where they’re headed. All the talk about our own intelligence - and that the Europeans will cover for American intelligence for us - turned out to be false. No one can replace American intelligence," he said in an interview with RBC-Ukraine.
The lawmaker criticized Ukrainian politicians, including Vladimir Zelensky, for making accusations in the media against US President Donald Trump. "Under such circumstances, a responsible politician has no right to attack the American president," he added.
Previously, Ukrainian military officials and politicians had repeatedly said that the United States was not fully providing data on ballistic missile launches, preventing Ukrainian air defense systems from effectively intercepting them.

articles.title: South Korea pulls diplomats from Ukraine
articles.body:
South Korea pulls diplomats from Ukraine
South Korea is withdrawing more diplomatic staff from Ukraine over Kiev’s failure to resolve a dispute sparked by Vladimir Zelensky’s disclosure of a secret North Korean prisoner transfer, the Foreign Ministry in Seoul has announced.
The dispute erupted after Zelensky publicly announced the transfer of two captured North Korean soldiers to Seoul during his address to the UN General Assembly in September. South Korea insists that the operation was supposed to remain confidential, while Ukrainian authorities deny that any such agreement existed.
The servicemen were reportedly captured in January 2025 in Russia’s Kursk Region, where North Korean troops helped Russian forces repel a Ukrainian incursion.
Foreign Ministry spokesman Park Doo-soon announced the withdrawal at a press briefing on Tuesday, saying that Kiev had failed to take “positive steps” to settle the dispute despite repeated diplomatic protests.
“This measure was taken because we judged it necessary to facilitate an amicable resolution of the issue and restore trust between the two countries,” Park told reporters.
He also cited persistent threats of airstrikes across Ukraine, saying they had made it difficult to guarantee the safety of diplomatic personnel.
Seoul did not disclose how many staff would be withdrawn. A chargé d’affaires will remain in Kiev to maintain diplomatic contacts, while consular personnel will continue assisting South Korean nationals.
South Korean President Lee Jae-myung accused Kiev of violating a confidentiality agreement intended to protect the prisoners and their families in North Korea. He warned that exposing the transfer could endanger their relatives and undermine stability on the Korean Peninsula, insisting that Ukraine itself had originally demanded secrecy.
Earlier this month, Lee warned that “if the Ukrainian government continues to refuse acknowledging the facts and issuing a public apology, we will take additional measures.”
The row deepened after Zelensky’s adviser Dmitry Litvin denied that any confidentiality agreement existed. Seoul summoned Ukraine’s acting ambassador to lodge a formal protest and demanded that Kiev acknowledge the arrangement and issue a public apology.
South Korea recalled its ambassador from Kiev on October 8 after its demands went unanswered. The move marked the first time in 18 years that Seoul had withdrawn an ambassador in a diplomatic protest. The latest decision further escalates the standoff, with South Korean media reporting that roughly half of the embassy staff are now expected to leave Kiev.
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrey Sibiga previously sought to downplay the row with Seoul, describing it as a “diplomatic misunderstanding” and saying that he was working to resolve it. He denied that Kiev had breached its commitments, attributing the dispute to differing interpretations of confidentiality arrangements.
Last week, Sibiga declared the matter closed, insisting Ukraine had fulfilled all its obligations. Seoul, however, said a message from Kiev containing words of apology fell short of what it expected.
South Korea has become a major arms exporter since the Ukraine conflict escalated in 2022, securing multibillion-dollar weapons deals with Poland. However, Seoul has refused to supply lethal weapons directly to Kiev, citing its longstanding policy against arming countries at war.
It has instead provided non-lethal military equipment, including helmets, bulletproof vests, and mine detectors, alongside humanitarian and financial aid.

articles.title: Rubio outraged by claims US no longer warns Ukraine of ballistic threats
articles.body:
Rubio outraged by claims US no longer warns Ukraine of ballistic threats
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has dismissed reports that the United States has stopped transmitting data on ballistic threats to Ukraine as false.
Source: European Pravda, citing Rubio speaking to journalists in India
Details: Rubio insists that the lack of warning about the launch of Russian ballistic missiles against Ukraine was an "internal issue" rather than a deliberate move by the US administration.
Quote: "I saw somebody associated with the Ukrainian government say that people in Ukraine are dying because the US is denying them information. That's scandalous. That's outrageous. That's just simply not true. That's not accurate."
Details: Rubio noted that he was referring to the Russian attacks on 13 and 18 October. The US is currently investigating the nature of the problem with the warnings.
Quote: "Now, that there was a problem identifying that, perhaps there was an internal issue in terms of them being able to take the information that was being provided and systematise it and react to it. That's possible. We're looking at it. Our understanding is that to the extent that happened on the 13th and on the 18th, it was a technical matter.
It was not the result of any sort of US directive not to provide advance warning of a strike. And we are providing the same warnings to them now that we always have."
Background:
- On Tuesday, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy spoke with Rubio to discuss the situation regarding Starlink, warnings about ballistic attacks, and air defence assistance.
- On 18 October, Zelenskyy said the US had resumed intelligence sharing with Ukraine to defend against Russian missile strikes.
- Meanwhile, Rubio insisted that there had previously been "software problems" on the Ukrainian side, which caused delays in notifications regarding ballistic threats.

articles.title: Vance refuses to call Ukraine an ally
articles.body:
Vance refuses to call Ukraine an ally
Vice President J.D. Vance refused to call Ukraine a US ally, noting that the two countries are at odds on a number of issues.
Asked by journalist Mark Halperin in an interview released on Monday whether Ukraine is a US ally, Vance suggested that Kiev is “certainly a partner” but noted that the countries “have some divergent interests from time to time.” 
“Do I think they should be bombing Russian diesel facilities that raise the cost of energy for Americans? No… I think they should stop bombing Russian energy.”
Pressed on the distinction between partner and ally, Vance said the US has no formal alliance with Ukraine. “They’re not in NATO. I don’t think that they should be in NATO,” he said. He added that the two countries will continue to work on some issues despite their differences.
The remarks come amid a rift between US President Donald Trump and Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky, which escalated after Trump announced a surprise deal to bring Russian diesel to the US and global markets following talks with President Vladimir Putin in early October.
Zelensky called the deal a “weak decision,” which came after Kiev ignored a number of US requests to stop attacking Russian refineries.
Zelensky refused to comply with Trump’s demand to end the strikes. The US president accused him of driving up fuel prices for Americans and said: “I think it’s time for Ukraine to get a new president.”
Zelensky’s presidential term expired in May 2024, but he refused to hold a new election, citing martial law. Russia has since declared Zelensky illegitimate, saying his status is an obstacle to signing a binding peace deal.
On Sunday, Trump accused Zelensky of not wanting the conflict with Russia to end, saying he “probably never did,” adding that Ukraine should “get somebody else to negotiate.”
Ukrainian officials also reported that they missed advance US warnings of Russian missile strikes and claimed there are new restrictions on the Starshield satellite service developed by SpaceX and used by Ukrainian drones. Media reports also suggested that the US threatened to stop intelligence sharing with Kiev, which US officials have denied.

US officials plan to travel to Norway, Russia for Ukraine talks, sources say

Another person familiar with the matter said Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner, who was expected to take part in the talks, was sick and would attend virtually.
