🔸 Donald Trump s’en prend violemment à la France, qu’il décrit comme une « grande nation d’autrefois » en train d’être « conquise, pillée et incendiée » par des « migrants, des djihadistes et des communistes » qui, selon lui, « haïssent le…
— Little Think Tank (@L_ThinkTank) October 20, 2026
The rally kicked off a six-day campaign blitz through Republican strongholds, with stops planned in the Carolinas, Florida, Iowa and Georgia, as Trump seeks to boost turnout and defend the party’s narrow congressional majorities. Democrats need to flip four seats in each chamber to overturn Republicans’ 218-214 House majority and 53-47 Senate advantage.
Trump’s bet on Russian diesel
Trump has also sought to shore up Republican support ahead of the midterms by tackling soaring fuel prices, as the Iran war and tariffs squeeze household budgets. A Reuters/Ipsos poll found that 68% of Americans disapprove of his handling of the economy, including 37% of Republicans.
To ease the pressure, Trump moved to lift sanctions on Russian diesel exports, blaming fuel shortages on Ukrainian strikes against Russian energy infrastructure rather than the Iran war and the de facto closure of the Strait of Hormuz.
The deal with Moscow would release over 300,000 tons of diesel immediately, another 500,000 tons in November and one million tons thereafter. Russian presidential aide Kirill Dmitriev told RT the agreement had an immediate “positive effect,” with New York diesel futures falling 5% on the announcement.
The move, however, drew accusations of “betraying Ukraine” from Democrats and some Republicans, who urged Trump to end the Iran war instead. He defended the deal as “the right choice for the American People” and later went further by invoking a national-interest exemption to suspend recently enacted Russia sanctions, including 500% tariffs on Russian imports and 100% tariffs on major buyers of Russian oil and gas.

articles.title: South Korea recalls some diplomatic staff from Ukraine over POW dispute
articles.body:
South Korea recalls some diplomatic staff from Ukraine over POW dispute
South Korea has decided to recall some of its diplomatic staff from Ukraine due to what Seoul considers a lack of positive steps by Kyiv to resolve a dispute over the public disclosure of information regarding the transfer of two North Korean prisoners of war, as well as the ongoing risk of Russian airstrikes.
Source: Yonhap, a South Korean news agency, citing Park Doo-soon, spokesperson for the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of South Korea
Details: Park Doo-soon said at a regular press briefing that Ukraine has yet to take "positive steps" to resolve the diplomatic dispute regarding Kyiv's unilateral disclosure of the news that two North Korean POWs had been transferred to Seoul, and that persistent threats of airstrikes make it difficult to ensure the safety of diplomatic personnel.
Despite this partial recall, the spokesperson noted that South Korea will maintain the necessary diplomatic contact with Ukraine led by a chargé d'affaires ad interim, adding that all consular staff will remain in the country to continue efforts to protect South Korean citizens.
Earlier in October, South Korea recalled its ambassador to Ukraine, Park Ki-chang, as Seoul expressed regret over Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's public disclosure of the transfer of the North Korean prisoners of war.
Seoul is demanding an official explanation and an apology from Ukraine regarding Zelenskyy's disclosure of the information. However, the Office of the President of Ukraine has denied that there was any agreement to maintain confidentiality on the matter.
Background:
- South Korean President Lee Jae-myung said Ukraine had breached a non-disclosure agreement by publicly revealing the transfer of the two North Korean POWs to South Korea and that making the information public could lead to numerous problems.
- Zelenskyy's communications adviser, Dmytro Lytvyn, denied that Ukraine had breached any non-disclosure agreement with South Korea.
- However, the South Korean president's office demanded an official explanation and apology from Ukraine for disclosing the transfer.

articles.title: Two re-arrested over alleged help to Iranian intelligence
articles.body:
Two men have been re-arrested in the investigation into activity close to RAF Fairford last month on suspicion of assisting a foreign intelligence service, with police confirming that the country the investigation relates to is Iran, according to a statement issued by Counter Terrorism Policing.
A 24-year-old United Kingdom national and a 25-year-old dual British and Iranian national, both from the London borough of Westminster, were re-arrested on Tuesday under Section 3 of the National Security Act 2023. The 24-year-old was first arrested on Sunday 27 September near the Gloucestershire base, and the 25-year-old was arrested in Westminster on Thursday 1 October.
Assistant Commissioner Laurence Taylor, head of National Counter Terrorism Policing in the United Kingdom, said: “Since the events at RAF Fairford on Sunday 27 September, our specialist teams have been working tirelessly to interrogate the many lines of enquiry involved in this hugely complex investigation.
“So far seven men have been arrested in connection with our investigation.
“As a result of the ongoing efforts of our officers, earlier today two of those men were re-arrested for offences relating to Section 3 of the National Security Act, assisting a foreign intelligence service.
“This is very much a live investigation, and our evidence gathering continues, but at this time our position remains the same; we consider it highly likely that there is Iranian state involvement. Our investigators are continuing to examine what that level of involvement was and the ambition behind it.
“Due to their sensitive nature, national security investigations can take time to progress, and I’m grateful to everyone who has given my teams the time and space needed to pursue this work thoroughly and effectively.
“From the outset our priority has been to uphold the integrity of this investigation and hold those who wish to do our country harm, accountable.
“We know the public have unanswered questions. I want to be as transparent as possible and when we are in the position to share more, we will.”
The other five men arrested remain on police bail.
Moving the two men onto Section 3 of the National Security Act marks a shift in how the case is being pursued. Five men in their twenties were arrested near Fairford on 27 September, and the Westminster arrest on 1 October was made under Section 5 of the Terrorism Act 2006, which covers preparing terrorist acts, with police saying at the time that they were considering all possible angles including foreign state involvement. The offence now under investigation is one of working for another country’s intelligence service.
Section 3 was created by the National Security Act 2023, which replaced the Official Secrets Acts and built a modern framework around espionage, sabotage and foreign interference. The offence carries a maximum sentence of fourteen years and applies where a person engages in conduct intended to materially assist a foreign intelligence service, including inside the United Kingdom.
RAF Fairford is a standby base operated by the United States Air Force under British ownership, with a runway long enough for the heaviest American aircraft, and it has hosted B-2 Spirit and B-52 bomber deployments to Europe for decades. It has no permanently based flying units, which is precisely what makes it useful when American bombers are sent across the Atlantic at short notice.
Louise Sandher-Jones, the Minister for the Armed Forces, told Parliament this week that security had been strengthened following the events at Fairford and at RAF Molesworth, that the Defence Investment Plan provides an additional £470 million over four years for site protection, and that the department would not hesitate to use the full range of powers available including the National Security Act.
Iran has been the subject of repeated British counter terrorism and national security operations in recent years, with MI5 having said publicly that it has disrupted a large number of plots linked to the Iranian state on British soil since 2022. None of the seven men has been charged.

Russia is waiting for responses from the United States regarding issues related to the development of biological weapons in Ukraine with the support of the Pentagon, Kirill Vorontsov, deputy head of the Russian delegation and deputy director of the Department for Non-Proliferation and Arms Control at the Russian Foreign Ministry has said.
"Legitimate questions, officially raised by Russia, remain unanswered. These questions concern the uncovered facts regarding the implementation of a military-biological program in Ukraine - in violation of the Biological Weapons Convention - with the support of the US Department of Defense and its affiliated entities, including private companies," he said during a discussion on Other Weapons of Mass Destruction within the First Committee of the 81st session of the UN General Assembly. A transcript of his remarks has been published on the Russian Foreign Ministry’s website.
As Vorontsov noted, "an analysis of the projects carried out in Ukrainian laboratories leads to the conclusion that components of biological weapons were, or perhaps still are, being developed in the immediate vicinity of Russian territory." He emphasized that Russia views this as a direct threat to its national security.
"The admission - cited by Tulsi Gabbard - regarding Washington’s long-term funding of 'potentially risky' virus experiments in over 120 foreign biolaboratories - more than 40 of which are located in Ukraine - only confirms the validity of Russia’s concerns regarding American military-biological activity near our borders," Vorontsov pointed out. "We expect the United States, as one of the depositaries of the BTWC, to provide appropriate responses to the questions we have raised. This would help resolve this unsavory situation and ensure that Washington complies with the obligations stipulated by the Convention," he concluded.

articles.title: Trump's backing of Netanyahu, Hegseth's secret visit fuel Iran war fears ahead of Israel's election
articles.body:
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu insists he promised U.S. President Donald Trump nothing in return for his public endorsement ahead of Israel's October 27 election. But with Trump, political gifts rarely come without expectations. For Netanyahu, whose ultimate ambition remains the fall of Iran's Islamic Republic, the American president's support may come at a price, potentially requiring Israeli concessions on other issues, particularly Washington's 20-point plan for Gaza.
One such concession is already taking shape. Netanyahu has agreed to the establishment of an "Emirati bubble" in Gaza, where reconstruction could begin before the Strip is demilitarized and Hamas is disarmed. The arrangement suggests the prime minister may be prepared to accommodate Trump on Gaza if doing so helps secure American backing for what he considers his defining strategic objective: bringing down the regime in Tehran.
The timing of Trump's endorsement, followed by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth's unannounced visit to Israel, has sharpened speculation about the possibility of another round of fighting with Iran. Netanyahu has repeatedly described the confrontation with Tehran as his life's work and said in recent days that he instructed Israel's defense establishment to bring down the Iranian regime.
Hegseth had been scheduled to visit Israel in July, but that trip was canceled at the last moment. His arrival now, just eight days before Israelis go to the polls, comes amid discussions about the possible resumption of major military operations against Iran. The proximity of the visit to Trump's endorsement has added to questions about Washington's intentions and Netanyahu's calculations.
Yet one senior Israeli official offers a markedly different interpretation. According to the official, Netanyahu is eager to attack Iran but cannot currently do so because Israel lacks the necessary intelligence. The Americans, the official said, are not interested in another strike at this stage, and Hegseth did not come to coordinate an operation. Rather, the purpose of his visit was to ensure Netanyahu was not preparing any surprises before the U.S. midterm elections on November 3.
That assessment illustrates the competing interests at play. Netanyahu sees regime change in Iran as the ultimate strategic prize, while the Trump administration must weigh the consequences of another confrontation against its own political timetable. For both leaders, the coming weeks carry significant military and political risks.
The danger of an Iranian preemptive strike
The increasingly heated rhetoric could itself become a trigger for war. With Israeli leaders issuing warnings, security consultations taking place late into the night and Hegseth making an unannounced visit, Iranian officials could conclude that Israel is preparing an imminent attack. Tehran might then attempt to strike first, setting off a rapid escalation that neither side had necessarily intended to initiate at that moment.
Israel's message in recent days has been consistent: If Iran makes a mistake, the Israeli response will be unprecedented. The warning appears to refer not only to the scale of a possible operation but also to the targets Israel could choose. Previous reports have indicated that Israeli planners considered striking Iranian infrastructure and energy facilities in the belief that such attacks could accelerate the collapse of the regime.
But the central assumption remains uncertain. Even another devastating military campaign would not guarantee the fall of Iran's leadership. As one Israeli source put it, nobody is promising that this time the regime in Tehran will collapse.
The costs of another war would also extend well beyond the battlefield. Israel would face the prospect of extensive damage to civilian infrastructure, a prolonged reconstruction effort and potentially significant casualties. During Operation Roaring Lion, 30 Israeli civilians were killed by direct Iranian missile strikes, while 12 soldiers and one civilian were killed on the Lebanese front. Another major confrontation could expose the Israeli home front to further missile attacks.
The election timetable adds another layer of complexity. IDF Chief of Staff Lt. Gen. Eyal Zamir has made clear to American officials that renewed fighting before October 27 could force Israel to postpone its election. A military confrontation in the final days of the campaign would therefore have consequences extending beyond national security, potentially disrupting the country's democratic process.
An Israeli source familiar with the situation put the chances of renewed fighting before the election at 30%, compared with a 70% likelihood that war would not resume before October 27. The figures represent that source's assessment rather than a certainty about either side's intentions.
The next deadline is November 3, when Americans vote in the midterm elections. Trump has indicated that the confrontation with Iran would be brought to a conclusion after that date, one way or another. As a result, the timing of any possible military operation is being considered against two closely spaced elections, each carrying its own political constraints.
Opposition questions Netanyahu's motives
Within Israel's opposition, the renewed discussion of war with Iran has prompted suspicion that political considerations may be influencing the timing and intensity of Netanyahu's warnings. Opposition figures believe the atmosphere of urgency surrounding the Iranian threat may serve the prime minister's interests in the final days of the campaign.
The signals have been difficult to ignore: late-night security consultations, briefings suggesting Iran could attempt to disrupt Israel's election and the unannounced arrival of Hegseth, widely regarded as one of the more hawkish members of Trump's administration. Together, they have contributed to the impression that another confrontation could be approaching.
There is also the question of who within Israel's security establishment might challenge the prime minister's calculations. Zamir appears to be the senior defense official most likely to scrutinize the timing and motives behind a proposed operation. The heads of Mossad, the National Security Council and Shin Bet are all Netanyahu appointees, although their appointments do not establish how they would respond to a decision to strike.
For Israel to initiate a discretionary war against Iran, Netanyahu would need Security Cabinet approval. An Iranian preemptive attack, however, could fundamentally change the circumstances, turning the question from whether Israel should launch a new operation into how it should respond to an attack already underway.
That is where the greatest danger may lie. Netanyahu's determination to bring down the Iranian regime, Trump's political backing and the signals surrounding Hegseth's visit have created an atmosphere in which intentions can easily be misread. Even if Washington and Jerusalem ultimately decide against launching an operation before the elections, Tehran could reach a different conclusion and act first. The result could be a war triggered not by a carefully coordinated decision, but by a miscalculation at one of the most politically sensitive moments for both Israel and the United States.

articles.title: Death toll from Houthi strike on Yemen govt camp rises to 73

Death toll from Houthi strike on Yemen govt camp rises to 73
Local Yemeni authorities on Tuesday raised the death toll from a Houthi strike a day earlier on a military camp belonging to government forces to 73, as fighting between the foes escalates.
It marked the deadliest attack in weeks as fighting between the Iran-backed Houthis and Yemen's internationally recognised, Saudi-supported government rages after the collapse of a years-long truce.
The death toll from Monday's strike on the camp in the energy-rich Shabwa province "increased to 73 martyrs, while search and follow-up efforts are ongoing to discover the fate of 14 missing people", provincial authorities said in a statement.
Local authorities had put the death toll at 53 on Monday, adding that more than 200 others were injured, all new members of the internal security forces who were undergoing training.
Majed al-Nuzaili, spokesperson for the Yemeni armed forces, stated Monday on X that the Houthis targeted Shabwa with three ballistic missiles, and that the attack "struck a training center for personnel of security and police agencies."
Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree later confirmed that the group was responsible for the attack, saying it targeted "Saudi enemy gatherings in Al-Alam camp, which is run by a Saudi officer from the eastern regions".
Shabwa contains major oil and gas fields and is home to the Balhaf liquefied natural gas terminal, the country's largest energy facility and a key economic asset.
A government military source in the province on Monday said the army feared the strikes could pave the way for a ground offensive "similar to what happened in Mokha", the strategic Red Sea port city seized by the Houthis last month.
(AFP)

articles.title: Lebanon judge to question Hezbollah officials over explosives
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Lebanon judge to question Hezbollah officials over explosives shipment
A Lebanese judge on Tuesday ordered two Hezbollah officials to appear for questioning over their alleged involvement in a delivery of explosives seized by authorities this month, a judicial official told AFP.
Lebanese authorities had been carrying out investigations after arresting two suspected Hezbollah members accused of transporting half a tonne of explosives, which the Iran-backed group subsequently said were part of its "capabilities" to be used against Israel.
They were caught on October 8 at a security checkpoint in Dahr al-Baidar in Lebanon's east in a vehicle headed towards Beirut, with a source telling AFP that one was the son of a Hezbollah official and the other was also a group member.
The judicial official, requesting anonymity, told AFP that the judge on Tuesday ordered two Hezbollah officials to appear for questioning "after initial investigations... established their identities".
Security agencies are working to locate them and take them into custody, the official added.
Last week, Hezbollah lawmaker Hassan Fadlallah said the explosives belonged to the militant group, demanding the shipment be returned and calling for those arrested to be released, in a rare admission by the group.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio subsequently urged Lebanon not to return the explosives.
Lebanese authorities have announced the seizure of three large shipments of explosives this month alone.
Lebanese Prime Minister Nawaf Salam has vowed that authorities "will deal with weapons outside the legal framework with the required firmness".
President Joseph Aoun on Saturday said the army and security forces were "implementing the government's decisions on extending the state's authority... and confiscating weapons and ammunition".
"Violators are referred to the judiciary, which carries out its duties fully in applying the law and the political authorities' decisions," he added.
Lebanese authorities last year committed to disarming Hezbollah after months of cross-border hostilities culminated in a 2024 war between the group and Israel.
But Hezbollah drew Lebanon into the Middle East war this year by attacking Israel, which responded with heavy strikes and a ground invasion.
In June, Lebanese and Israeli authorities signed a framework agreement which involves the disarmament of Hezbollah, a gradual Israeli withdrawal from territories it occupies, and the deployment of the Lebanese army to the area.
Hezbollah, the only militant group that refused to disarm after Lebanon's 1975-1990 civil war, has rejected surrendering its weapons and the direct negotiations with Israel.
(AFP)

European Parliament Vice President Pina Picierno announces hunger strike to draw international attention to civilians trapped in Russian-occupied Oleshky, Ukraine
European Parliament Vice President Pina Picierno announced a hunger strike to “draw international attention” to the situation in Oleshky, a city in the occupied part of Ukraine’s Kherson region.
Picierno called on humanitarian organizations and governments to take notice of her protest.
“We must demand an immediate humanitarian truce, the entry of food and medicines, and the possibility of safely evacuating civilians who wish to leave the city,” she said.
Oleshky is under Russian control. For months, its residents have been without electricity, food, and adequate medical care amid relentless shelling from both sides. Leaving the city is nearly impossible because most roads out are mined.
Several days ago, Pope Leo XIV called Russian President Vladimir Putin to ask him to ensure that humanitarian aid could reach the city and residents could be evacuated. Soon afterward, Dmytro Lubinets, the Ukrainian Parliament’s human rights commissioner, confirmed that Kyiv and Moscow were working to resolve the situation. articles.title: Witkoff hopes to visit Russia after meeting Zelensky in Oslo — Axios reporter
articles.body:
WASHINGTON, October 20. /TASS/. US Presidential Special Envoy Steve Witkoff hopes to visit Russia and meet with Russian President Vladimir Putin after holding talks with Vladimir Zelensky in Oslo on Tuesday, Barak Ravid, a correspondent for Axios and Israel’s Channel 12, said on X, citing sources.
According to the sources, Witkoff is currently flying to Oslo for a meeting with Zelensky scheduled for Tuesday. Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store, as well as representatives of the United Kingdom, Germany, Italy, France, the European Union leadership, and NATO, are expected to take part in the talks.
"The objective is to continue aligning on a comprehensive proposal that can form the basis for renewed negotiations with Russia," Ravid said.
According to one of his sources, Witkoff hopes to visit Russia after Oslo, where he intends to discuss with Putin the proposals developed jointly with Ukraine and European partners. Last week, representatives of the United States, Ukraine, and Europe worked on developing these proposals at the technical level. They include the release of Stephen Hubbard, a 72-year-old US citizen convicted in Russia of fighting on the side of the Ukrainian armed forces.
"President Trump has directed an intensive process to develop a comprehensive peace proposal with Ukraine and Europe, and the next step is to test whether that work can form the basis for serious negotiations with Russia", a US official told Ravid, adding. "These discussions remain fluid, and substantial work remains. President Trump’s objective is clear: to end the killing, bring the war to a close, and establish the conditions for a lasting peace that benefits Ukraine, Russia, Europe, and the United States."
Jared Kushner, a special envoy and son-in-law of the US president, will not accompany Witkoff in person this time because he has the flu. He will participate in the consultations remotely.
On October 1, Putin said Russia would like to end hostilities in Ukraine through a peaceful settlement as soon as possible. Moscow is ready for negotiations but sees no willingness on the part of the Kiev government to engage in talks, the president added.

articles.title: Ukraine's HUR claims 108 Russian soldiers killed, 29 captured in Sumy Oblast operation
articles.body:
Ukraine's HUR claims 108 Russian soldiers killed, 29 captured in Sumy Oblast operation
Ukrainian special forces killed 108 Russian soldiers, captured another 29, and struck more than 1,100 Russian targets during a seven-week operation in Sumy Oblast, Ukraine's military intelligence (HUR) reported on Oct. 20.
According to HUR's Active Operations Department, the operation was carried out by its Group 10 special forces unit, which reportedly thwarted Russian offensive plans and prevented Russian troops from cutting off Ukrainian logistical routes in the region.
Over the course of seven weeks, Ukrainian operatives cleared Russian troops from more than 600 hectares of forest before handing over the positions to Ukraine's Defense Forces, the intelligence agency said.
HUR did not specify the exact location of the operation or when it took place.
The Kyiv Independent could not independently verify these claims.
Ukraine's defensive operations reduced the pace of Russia's territorial advances by more than half in the first six months of 2026, then-Commander-in-Chief Oleksandr Syrskyi said on July 10.
Separately, on Sept. 28, Ukraine's 3rd Army Corps reported further territorial gains in northern Donetsk Oblast as part of Operation Vivaldi, a counteroffensive that had reclaimed a total of 176 square kilometers. According to the corps, the latest phase of the operation inflicted more than 2,000 Russian casualties and resulted in the capture of over 250 Russian soldiers.

articles.title: Israel seeks to cast Lebanon army as 'failing' ahead of US talks
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Israel seeks to portray Lebanese army as failing to curb Hezbollah ahead of talks
Hours before Lebanon and Israel were due to resume negotiations in the United States, the Israeli military on Tuesday accused the Lebanese army of failing to curb Hezbollah’s activities in southern Lebanon, in what a retired Lebanese brigadier general described to The New Arab as an attempt to heighten tensions ahead of the talks and put Lebanon on the defensive.
The Israeli military accused elements within the Lebanese army of allegedly coordinating with Hezbollah to obstruct the enforcement of security arrangements, reportedly allowing the group to anticipate operations and move weapons out of targeted areas. It said the Lebanese army had also failed to dismantle a Hezbollah military site in the south, despite announcing that it had taken the necessary measures there.
The Israeli military said that the Lebanese army was responsible for ensuring the full implementation of the security arrangements, saying it expected it to take more decisive and effective measures to prevent Hezbollah from maintaining weapons and military infrastructure in southern Lebanon.
The Lebanese army later rejected the claims, describing them as false and accusing Israel of seeking to undermine its credibility and cast doubt on its ability to carry out its responsibilities in southern Lebanon.
Lebanon and Israel are due to hold technical military talks in Tampa, Florida, on Tuesday, resuming discussions after the last round of talks in Rome in early August. An eighth round planned for September in the Italian capital did not take place.
The Lebanese delegation is expected to reiterate its demands for a full Israeli withdrawal from southern Lebanon, which continues to come under daily Israeli attack despite a framework agreement signed in June.
Pressure on the Lebanese army
Retired Lebanese Brig. Gen. Bassam Yassin described the Israeli accusations as an attempt to undermine the talks and put the Lebanese army on the defensive.
"The intention is certainly to create tension around the negotiations and put the army in a position where it has to defend itself," Yassin told The New Arab.
He said the Lebanese delegation was expected to focus on technical issues, including the work of the ceasefire monitoring committee, locally known as the mechanism, and demands for an Israeli withdrawal.
The mechanism was established following the November 2024 ceasefire agreement between Israel and Hezbollah.
"All this talk about the army’s failure does not reflect the major successes it achieved south of the Litani River in 2024 and 2025," Yassin said, questioning why the alleged violations had not been raised with the mechanism at the time.
In a statement on Tuesday, the Israeli military said it expected the Lebanese army to take "more decisive and effective action" to prevent Hezbollah from maintaining weapons and military infrastructure in the south.
It alleged that, despite the Lebanese army announcing in December 2025 that it had dealt with a Hezbollah facility in the southern town of Kafra, footage showed members of the group continuing to operate there and attempting to remove weapons from the site months later.
The Israeli military said its forces had subsequently struck and destroyed a truck carrying the weapons. It also accused members of the Lebanese army of coordinating with Hezbollah over enforcement operations, allowing the group to anticipate military activity and move weapons out of targeted areas.
Yassin rejected the suggestion that the Lebanese army was failing to carry out its responsibilities. While the Lebanese government has made dismantling Hezbollah’s military infrastructure and disbanding its armed wing in the south a stated objective, he argued that the army could not be expected to forcibly disarm the group while Israeli forces continued to occupy Lebanese territory and carry out attacks.
"Of course, the army is not going to dismantle Hezbollah’s weapons and infrastructure in the south right now. There is an occupation and aggression on your land. Can the army confront civilians and tell them: ‘I want to dismantle your defences’? That is impossible," he said.
Yassin maintained that the army had taken control of every Hezbollah site it had entered following the November 2024 ceasefire, and said Hezbollah had helped it access many of its former positions.
Some sites were empty when the army arrived, while others were discovered by chance or with the help of local residents, he said. Some of the people responsible for those sites had been killed during the 2024 war, he added, meaning information about their locations was no longer available.
Yassin said the Israeli military's publication of footage now was intended to undermine confidence in the Lebanese army and portray it as weak.
"If there is something old [still there], that does not mean the Israelis can release videos now. The intention is to confuse the Lebanese army and portray it as being in a weak position, when that is not the case," he said.
Lebanese army rejects allegations
In a statement shared with footage on X, the army said its units had begun work on a military facility in the southern town of Kafra in December 2025. They continued working there until 16 March 2026, when they suspended operations and evacuated the area at the request of the mechanism, following Israeli threats to strike the site.
The army said it had informed the committee that the operation was incomplete and that military equipment and ammunition remained inside the facility, which was subsequently targeted by an Israeli strike. It added that repeated requests to secure permission to resume work and remove the remaining equipment had been rejected by Israel.
According to the statement, the army resumed its operation on 15 August 2026 in coordination with the mechanism, eventually completing the work and closing the facility on 16 October.
The Lebanese army also disputed the Israeli military's account of the footage showing a truck carrying weapons being struck. It said the video dated back to 3 July 2026 and was filmed in the village of Seddiqin rather than at the Kafra facility.
The army said all the events and measures it described had been documented with the mechanism, adding that Israel's repeated allegations and disinformation campaigns were aimed at damaging the military institution's credibility locally and internationally, particularly amid the ongoing negotiations.
It reiterated its commitment to carrying out its responsibilities and assigned tasks, while accusing Israel of continuing to violate existing understandings.
No progress on pilot zones
The talks are due to take place under US auspices against a backdrop of continued Israeli strikes and demolitions in southern Lebanon and growing concerns in Beirut about the consequences of a possible wider confrontation involving the United States, Israel and Iran.
A US official, in remarks carried by the US embassy in Beirut, said the meeting would be limited to working-level teams and focus exclusively on security issues within the tripartite framework signed by Lebanon and Israel in Washington on 26 June 2026.
Little progress has been made on the initial pilot areas announced under the arrangements this summer. Lebanese military sources told The New Arab that continued Israeli attacks were obstructing the army’s work in the areas and making the return of residents difficult and dangerous.
Beirut also rejects any direct coordination between the Lebanese and Israeli armies, despite pressure from Washington and Tel Aviv. Lebanon continues to pursue the diplomatic track, viewing it as the only viable option to end the conflict.
Fears of a more devastating war
Lebanese official sources told The New Arab that President Joseph Aoun was monitoring developments in the region and feared the consequences of any escalation for Lebanon. They said these concerns had also been raised by international officials and diplomats visiting Beirut, including Arab League Secretary-General Nabil Fahmy, who met Aoun on Monday.
The sources also expressed concern about Hezbollah’s increasingly confrontational position, warning that it could draw Lebanon into another war.
They said Lebanese officials were holding internal consultations through their advisers to convey their concerns and urged all sides to put Lebanon’s interests above external agendas.
The sources added that officials had received warnings that another war could have even more serious consequences than the previous rounds of fighting in October 2023 and March 2026.
Hezbollah and Israel began exchanging fire in October 2023, with the conflict escalating into a full-scale war in September 2024. Fighting resumed on 2 March 2026 following the start of the US-Israel war on Iran.
Although fighting largely subsided in June following the signing of the tripartite framework, Israel has continued attacks and demolitions in its so-called buffer zone in southern Lebanon, occupying strategic sites and destroying Hezbollah tunnels.
Israeli attacks over the past three years have killed 8,596 people and wounded more than 30,660 others, many of them civilians.

articles.title: Zelenskyy: In any case, we have more in common than US and Russia do
articles.body:
Zelenskyy: US has more in common with Ukraine than with Russia
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said he believes that Ukraine and the US have more in common than Russia and the US, and that Ukraine would like to continue to have an open, pragmatic and honest relationship with the United States.
Source: Zelenskyy in an interview with Corriere della Sera
Quote: "We have always had important, strong strategic relations with the United States of America. Our bilateral relationship began developing particularly actively during the full-scale war. I am grateful for all the support.
But we have always built our relationship on honesty, fairness and, most importantly, transparency. Because when you lie while your people are at war, it is very painful. That is why I have always wanted to hide nothing and never lie to the president of the United States.
In any case, we have more in common than America does with Russia. Most people in Ukraine and the United States of America understand this.
We would like to continue having the same open, honest, and pragmatic relations with America that we have today."
Details: Zelenskyy added that Ukraine is in favour of a mutual energy ceasefire and said that if Russia ignored it, Ukraine's partners could provide enough air defence systems to enable the country to protect its energy infrastructure.
Quote: "The position is very simple. We support a mutual energy ceasefire. If we are talking about the idea that we should not strike back at Russian energy facilities after they strike our gas, electricity, oil – everything. The Russians are striking. America cannot stop them.
Let's believe that America really wants to but cannot. Then, as a partner, I am willing to meet President Trump halfway: if they strike us and we cannot strike back – that is neither honest nor fair – but if this is what you need, if you cannot rein Putin in, then give us interceptor missiles so I can protect our energy infrastructure. You couldn't stop Putin – but you helped Ukraine."
Background:
- On Sunday 18 October, Zelenskyy accused US President Donald Trump of trying to pressure Ukraine into capitulating to Russia and of delaying deliveries of Patriot interceptor missiles.
- Trump accused Zelenskyy of never having wanted to end Russia's war against Ukraine.
- On 19 October, Trump said he is willing to meet Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping to discuss ending the war in Ukraine, even without Zelenskyy taking part.

articles.title: South Sudan accuses neighbor of deadly drone strike
articles.body:
South Sudan accuses neighbor of deadly drone strike
South Sudan has accused neighboring Sudan of carrying out a drone strike on a market in the disputed Abyei region which reportedly killed 73 people and injured 19 others.
The South Sudanese Foreign Ministry said on Monday that it had summoned Sudanese Ambassador Essam Mohamed Karrar to express its strong objection to the attack on Amiet Market, located north of Abyei town.
“The Government of the Republic of South Sudan has learned with grave concern of the drone attack carried out by the Sudanese Armed Forces against Amiet Market, situated north of Abyei Town,” the ministry said. However, officials in Juba and Abyei did not provide direct evidence pinning the strike on the Sudanese Army. The Sudanese government has not publicly commented on the allegations.
Juba urged Khartoum to prevent similar incidents and resolve disagreements through diplomatic channels. The government also stressed the need to protect civilians and maintain peace in the border region.
The attack took place on Monday morning, hitting several sections of the market, including its northern entrance. At least 73 people were killed and 19 injured in the attack, Abyei’s information minister, Yohana Akol Ngor, told Radio Tamazuj.
An anonymous diplomatic source and an aid worker told Reuters that the strike hit a fuel depot at the market. The facility had previously been used to supply Sudan’s paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF), the source added.
Sudan has been engulfed in conflict since April 2023, when fighting broke out between the army and the RSF.
Sudan descended into chaos in April 2023 when fighting erupted between the national army, the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF), and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF). The conflict followed months of tension between their commanders, Abdel Fattah al-Burhan and Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo, known as Hemedti, over a planned transition to civilian rule. What began in the capital, Khartoum, as a power struggle has devastated the country, killing tens of thousands, displacing millions, and pushing parts of Sudan into famine.
Regional and international peace efforts, including African Union mediation and Saudi-US talks in Jeddah, have repeatedly stalled. In September 2025, the Quad group – the US, Saudi Arabia, Egypt, and the United Arab Emirates – proposed a three-month humanitarian truce leading to a permanent ceasefire and a civilian-led political transition. Burhan rejected a subsequent US-led proposal that November, arguing it would dismantle state security institutions while leaving the RSF in place. The paramilitaries said they accepted the truce.
The UAE’s involvement has deepened mistrust of mediation. Sudan’s army-backed government severed diplomatic ties with Abu Dhabi in May 2025, accusing it of supporting the RSF. The UAE denies supplying weapons to the paramilitaries. Relations with Washington deteriorated further in September 2026 after the US questioned both factions’ legitimacy. Sudan rejected the remarks and called for peace efforts free from foreign dictates.
Meanwhile, rival administrations have entrenched Sudan’s divisions. Burhan’s government returned to Khartoum in January 2026 after the army recaptured the capital, having operated from Port Sudan during the fighting. In July 2025, the RSF-aligned TASIS coalition announced a rival government based in Nyala, Darfur, with Dagalo heading its governing council. The UN Security Council and African Union rejected the move.
Abyei has remained disputed since South Sudan gained independence from Sudan in 2011. The UN maintains a peacekeeping mission in the area, known as UNISFA, to help prevent violence.
South Sudan has been plagued by political instability and armed conflict since gaining independence in 2011. A five-year civil war erupted in 2013 over a feud between President Salva Kiir Mayardit and former First Vice President Riek Machar, rooted in power struggles within the ruling Sudan People’s Liberation Movement (SPLM – the party was founded in Sudan in 1983 and still keeps the same name). The 2018 peace agreement formally ended the civil war, but clashes continue across the country, driven by local militias and resource disputes.
The situation has been further complicated by political upheaval, including the arrest of Machar in March 2025. Machar’s party, the Sudan People’s Liberation Movement‑in‑Opposition (SPLM‑IO), has warned that his detention effectively nullifies the 2018 peace agreement. Machar has been accused of supporting the White Army, a militia composed largely of Nuer fighters, which reportedly participated in clashes in Upper Nile state.
Ongoing insecurity has displaced hundreds of thousands, worsening the humanitarian crisis. According to the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA), by the end of 2025, South Sudan had over 2.7 million internally displaced persons, and more than 9 million people in total are in need of humanitarian assistance.
In May, Russia’s deputy permanent representative to the UN, Anna Evstigneeva, warned that armed groups were obstructing efforts to settle Abyei’s status. Addressing the UN Security Council, she said RSF activity and continued fighting in neighboring areas were worsening security conditions. “It is the actions of elements opposing Khartoum that are the main obstacle to the start of a comprehensive settlement process,” Evstigneeva said.

articles.title: Britain sends Typhoon jets to shield Saudi skies from Houthi drones, missiles
articles.body:
Britain sends Typhoon jets to shield Saudi skies from Houthi drones, missiles
LONDON – Britain will fly Royal Air Force Typhoon fighter jets on defensive missions to help protect Saudi cities and critical national infrastructure from Houthi aerial attacks, the Ministry of Defence said on Oct 20.
The ministry said the warplanes would operate only in a defensive role and would not conduct offensive strikes against the Iran-aligned Houthis, whose attacks Britain says threaten regional stability and risk disrupting energy supplies and trade routes.
“The continuing attacks from the Houthis on our ally Saudi Arabia are absolutely despicable. The targeting of the airport in Riyadh, in particular, shows the lengths the Houthis are going to escalate the situation in the region,” Defence Minister Wes Streeting said in a statement.
“That’s why today I have approved further UK military support,” he said. “RAF Typhoons will fly defensive air missions to help protect Saudi airspace from drones and missiles.”
The additional support follows a request from Saudi Arabia’s government, which Prime Minister Andy Burnham said earlier in October Britain was prepared to consider.
Britain will also deploy an Atlas A400M transport aircraft and military advisers, expanding assistance announced in September that included an RAF Voyager air-to-air refuelling aircraft but not fighter jets.
Houthi attacks against Saudi oil facilities and other infrastructure have intensified in recent weeks as the conflict in Yemen has escalated.
Inside Yemen, the authorities said a Houthi strike on Oct 19 against a training camp for Saudi-backed government security forces killed 58 people. REUTERS

articles.title: Russia Attacked Ukraine’s Energy Sector Every Day Since Mid-July—With Over 2000 Strikes
articles.body:
- Category
- War in Ukraine
Russia Attacked Ukraine’s Energy Sector Every Day Since Mid-July—With Over 2000 Strikes
Russia has carried out 2,147 attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure since July 16, with strikes recorded every day, according to Ukraine’s Cabinet of Ministers on October 19.
Ukrainian Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi revealed the figures in an interview with BBC Ukraine, warning of intensifying Russian strikes ahead of winter. He stressed that not a single day had passed without attacks on the country's energy sector since the renewed government took office on July 16.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Koretskyi noted that the number of strikes was several times higher than during the comparable period last year. Russian forces are targeting electricity, heating, and water infrastructure, attempting to disrupt essential services before winter begins. He added that protective measures implemented under Ukraine's resilience plans have helped the energy system withstand repeated attacks.
“The Government's strategy remains unchanged. We are protecting everything that can be protected and expanding distributed generation,” Koretskyi stated. He explained that Ukraine is working with international partners to stockpile replacement transformers and other equipment, allowing damaged infrastructure to be restored more quickly.
The government is also strengthening backup power supplies for critical facilities, including water pumping stations, to maintain essential services during outages. Koretskyi noted that energy workers, utility crews, and emergency responders frequently conduct repairs under the threat of renewed Russian strikes.
He urged Ukrainians to use government assistance programs to install household backup power systems where possible, warning that the approaching winter requires serious preparation as Russia continues targeting essential infrastructure.
The warnings come as Ukraine braces for what could be Russia's most ambitious winter campaign yet against its power, heating, and water systems.
A document presented to European partners as an intercepted Russian plan outlines the use of up to 1,000 missiles, drones, and guided bombs against substations, power plants, and switchyards linking Ukraine's three operating nuclear plants to the grid.
It names Kyiv, Kharkiv, and Odesa as priority targets and estimates that the campaign could eliminate nearly 15 gigawatts of generating capacity. Before dawn on September 30, missiles and drones struck a major thermal power plant, leaving parts of Kyiv without electricity and water.

articles.title: Russian occupation official suspected of persecuting Ukrainian Greek Catholic priests
articles.body:
Russian occupation official suspected of persecuting Ukrainian Greek Catholic priests
A representative of the Russian occupation administration has been served with a notice of suspicion over the forced expulsion of Ukrainian Greek Catholic priests from temporarily occupied Melitopol.
Source: Office of the Prosecutor General on Facebook
Details: In 2024, the suspect was an authorised representative of Vladimir Putin in the presidential election, the Prosecutor General's Office reported.
The Book of Executioners, a Ukrainian project documenting Russian war criminals and those who betrayed Ukraine, says the suspect is Artem Sharlai, a native of Zaporizhzhia who has actively supported Russia since the beginning of the war in Ukraine's east.
Investigators say the suspect worked with Russian troops and officers of Russia's Federal Security Service (FSB) to persecute clergy with pro-Ukrainian views.
Quote: "He demanded that services in Ukrainian be stopped, that Ukrainian military personnel no longer be mentioned in prayers, that ties with religious organisations in Ukraine be severed and that congregations be re-registered under Russian law.
He also collected information about pro-Ukrainian priests and passed it on to FSB officers for further persecution."
Details: In December 2022, Sharlai personally took part in a search of a Greek Catholic parish and directed the search for religious literature deemed "extremist". This material was subsequently used as grounds for detention.
The investigators believe the suspect's actions facilitated the unlawful expulsion of Ukrainian Greek Catholic Church clergy, who are protected under international humanitarian law. He is accused of violating the laws and customs of war under Article 438.1 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine.
Background: Russian authorities in Crimea have recently sentenced a Ukrainian couple for alleged treason and preparations for terrorist attacks.

articles.title: NATO to send planes and drones to Black Sea after attacks on shipping
articles.body:
NATO to send ‘additional assets’ to Black Sea after drone attacks off Bulgaria, Romania
- NATO will send “additional assets” to the Black Sea, including surveillance, reconnaissance and forensics, after drone strikes near Romania and Bulgaria.
- Bulgaria said a US P-8 Poseidon has started patrols, and Sofia expects “further assistance” after the attacks on ships and missing sailors.
- EU diplomat Kaja Kallas called “six attacks in 10 days” a “dangerous and unacceptable escalation”, warning of risks to grain exports and global food supplies.
AI generated
BRUSSELS - NATO said on Oct 20 it will deploy “additional assets” to the Black Sea after a string of drone strikes off Romania and Bulgaria in the latest spillover from Russia’s war on Ukraine.
“NATO will be sending additional assets to the region, including support for surveillance, reconnaissance, and forensics,” NATO spokeswoman Allison Hart posted online, after a meeting of alliance ambassadors in Brussels.
“We will continue to stand united and ensure that we are ready and able to address any threat and to keep our one billion people safe,” she added.
The announcement from NATO came after Bulgaria’s Prime Minister Rumen Radev said that a US military plane had started to patrol the Black Sea following a plea for help after recent drone attacks.
“An American P-8 Poseidon... has begun patrolling the Black Sea to conduct reconnaissance missions and detect any activity that could pose a risk,” said Radev.
He said some NATO countries were quick to answer his call for help after the attacks and that Sofia expects “further assistance”.
The spate of strikes on ships in the waters off NATO and EU members Bulgaria and Romania have left more than a score of sailors missing and stirred condemnation in Europe.
The European Union’s top diplomat Kaja Kallas on Oct 20 said that “six attacks in 10 days by suspected Russian drones marks a dangerous and unacceptable escalation”.
Kallas accused the Kremlin of once again stepping up efforts to hit exports of Ukrainian grain via the Black Sea in a bid to starve Kyiv of revenues.
She warned that the latest strikes were adding to a “perfect storm” facing global food supplies already being battered by droughts in multiple regions and the war in the Middle East.
The attacks have also compounded worries at NATO over what is seen as increasingly reckless actions by Moscow at a time when its forces are bogged down in Ukraine.
NATO and the EU are grappling with what they say is a “hybrid” campaign of sabotage and interference by the Kremlin aimed at undercutting Western support for Kyiv.
NATO has sought to signal to Russia to tamp down its actions after high-profile incidents over the summer, including the discovery of an explosive-laden drone at a German airport. AFP

articles.title: NYT: Trump’s envoys plan to meet Putin in St. Petersburg on Wednesday and seek the release of an American held in Russia
articles.body:
NYT: Trump’s envoys plan to meet Putin in St. Petersburg on Wednesday and seek the release of an American held in Russia
President Donald Trump’s envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner plan to meet with Vladimir Putin in St. Petersburg on October 21, The New York Times reported.
Witkoff and Kushner are expected to take the next step in their efforts to “show the benefits of deal-making with Mr. Putin” by securing the release of “a long-held American.”
The report does not identify the American. The Times reported that the only American the U.S. State Department categorizes as “wrongfully detained” in Russia is Stephen Hubbard, who fought for the Ukrainian armed forces and was sentenced to six years and 10 months in a penal colony.
On October 20, Trump’s negotiators met with Volodymyr Zelensky in Oslo. No details of the meeting were available at the time of writing. Witkoff attended in person, while Kushner participated remotely because he had the flu. Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre and Finnish President Alexander Stubb also joined the meeting.
Stephen Hubbard is 72. In October 2024, a Russian court sentenced him to six years and 10 months in a standard-security penal colony on mercenary charges. Investigators alleged that Hubbard joined the territorial defense forces in Izium, in Ukraine’s Kharkiv region, in February 2022 (he had lived there since 2014), but was captured by Russian forces in April and later put on trial.
In April 2025, while the previous U.S. presidential administration was still in office, the State Department called on Russia to release Hubbard.

articles.title: Iran warns UN over Trump, Israel military threats
articles.body:
Iran's ambassador and chargé d'affaires to the United Nations, Gholamhossein Darzi, warned the UN secretary-general and the Security Council over what the letter called the "arrogant threats" of US President Donald Trump and the Zionist regime.
In the letter to UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres and the Security Council president, Darzi said the threats are part of US and Zionist regime wars of aggression against Iran that began on June 13, 2025 and Feb. 28, 2026, along with deliberate attacks on civilians and critical infrastructure. He said they risk further serious violations of international law with catastrophic humanitarian consequences and dangers to regional and international peace and security. He warned that responsibility rests with the United States, the Zionist regime and anyone who directly or indirectly supports their aggression and state terrorism.
The letter cited US media reports on Oct. 15, 2026 that the White House and Pentagon had prepared military options including the possible use of the GBU-43/B Massive Ordnance Air Blast, known as the "mother of all bombs," against Iran. It said Trump discussed the weapon in a television interview the same day and threatened Iran with further attacks.
It said Israeli war minister Yisrael Katz announced on Oct. 18, 2026 that Israel was ready to attack Iran and that in any new aggression "all energy facilities" would be targeted, with the aim of returning Iran to the "Stone Age." Katz also claimed the United States and Israel had dropped 35,000 bombs on Iran in total and said their military campaign was not over.
The letter said that on the same day, the Zionist regime's prime minister, who is a war criminal under international prosecution, again openly declared his criminal intent to preemptively start another war of aggression against Iran. It said the silence and explicit support of some Security Council members had made him more brazen in pursuing genocidal thinking.
The letter said the threats amount to gross violations of international law, including the threat to use the MOAB against civilian infrastructure and to target all of Iran's energy infrastructure. It said attempts to spread fear among Iran's population or any threat to deliberately destroy critical civilian infrastructure are new instances of gross violations of international humanitarian law with severe and possibly long-term humanitarian and environmental consequences, increasing the responsibility of the United States and the Zionist regime. It said both have repeatedly shown they do not consider themselves bound by any rules of international law, including obligations under the four 1949 Geneva Conventions and customary international humanitarian law.
Iran asked the UN secretary-general and the Security Council to demand that the United States and the Zionist regime immediately end their unlawful threats and fully comply with their obligations under the UN Charter and peremptory norms of international law. It also asked them to explicitly and unambiguously condemn threats to attack Iran, including its critical civilian infrastructure, used as a tool of coercion and intimidation.
Iran further urged the Security Council to take urgent measures within its powers and duties, including holding an emergency meeting to address the threats to regional and international peace and security and to ensure accountability for the United States and the rogue Zionist regime. It called on the Council to guarantee accountability and full compensation for damages caused by wrongful international acts that the United States and the Zionist regime commit against Iran daily.
The letter said the Security Council cannot remain silent in the face of explicit threats of further aggression and destruction of critical civilian infrastructure, warning that inaction would further weaken the Charter and the international legal order on which the UN system is built.
Iran reaffirmed its inherent right to self-defense under Article 51 of the UN Charter and its determination to take all necessary measures against any source of threat endangering its people, sovereignty, territorial integrity and vital national interests. It said that if the Security Council fails in its responsibilities, Iran will exercise its right of self-defense and give a decisive response in line with international law to protect its supreme national interests.
It said the United States and the Zionist regime will bear full responsibility for the consequences of any further aggression, including the risk of unpredictable and uncontrollable escalation.
Iran requested that the letter be distributed as an official document of the General Assembly and the Security Council.

articles.title: Turkey submits defense pact with Saudi Arabia, Pakistan to parliament for ratification, sources say
articles.body:
Turkey has submitted a defense pact with Pakistan and Saudi Arabia to parliament for ratification, three parliamentary sources said on Tuesday, moving NATO's second-largest army closer to a formal mutual defense pledge with Riyadh as it faces Houthi attacks.
The three countries signed the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement in August, under which an armed attack on one member is considered an attack on all. A joint statement issued when they signed the deal did not specify each country's commitments.
At an emergency meeting of the alliance in Riyadh earlier this month, they agreed to ensure the "rapid deployment" of military forces and capabilities in Saudi Arabia.
Turkey, which has a robust defense industry, has condemned Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, expressed willingness to help meet Riyadh's military technology needs and agreed to join a Saudi-led coalition to ensure navigational safety in the Red Sea.
Parliament must ratify the agreement for Turkey to formally approve it.
Parliament Speaker Numan Kurtulmus, currently visiting Kyrgyzstan, will refer the agreement to parliament's foreign affairs commission upon his return, two of the sources said. The contents and details of the agreement are expected to become public once it is submitted to the commission.
The commission could debate the agreement as early as Friday, another source said.
Turkish contribution to be limited to equipment, intelligence, official says
A Turkish official, who spoke on the condition of anonymity, said Turkey's own contribution was expected to be limited to military equipment, intelligence sharing, and weapons systems, adding that no other form of deployment had taken place under the alliance so far.
Asked how Turkey could help Saudi Arabia defend against attacks by Yemen's Houthis, Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said that the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement was not an "offensive agreement," adding that Turkey would not send troops to another country to carry out attacks on its territory.

articles.title: AI Adoption: Are Air Force and Space Force Ready and Willing?
articles.body:
Air Force and Space Force leaders are calling for Airmen and Guardians to enthusiastically embrace artificial intelligence and apply emerging tools to their work. In September, Chief Master Sergeant of the Air Force David Wolfe even went so far as to say those who don’t embrace AI “will end up in someone else’s rearview mirror.”
Secretary of the Air Force Troy Meink opened AFA’s annual Air, Space, and Cyber Conference Sept. 14 with the comments of a true believer, saying the department is “putting more than 300 AI tools into the hands of our people.”
“I use them every day,” Meink said. “This includes tools that streamline work for nearly 150,000 Airmen, and for our Guardians, data fusion tools that turn millions of data points into actual information.” He praised the maturing self-driving technology available in his personal automobile, and hinted that he was hard pressed to find a more complex problem for AI to solve than driving in downtown Washington D.C.
In June, following a “Corona” meeting of Air Force’s top three- and four-stars generals, Air Force Chief of Staff Gen. Kenneth Wilsbach announced forthcoming guidance for AI.
New Chief of Space Operations, Gen. Douglas A. Schiess noted even before he became Chief in September that his service was “not doing enough” to leverage AI. He stressed scaling AI across the force as a route to ensuring decision advantage. 
Yet despite leadership’s exhortations to embrace AI for automating burdensome admin tasks and accelerate decision-making, some experts see risk. “DOD’s approach to AI has been very interesting,” said Leah Siskind, an AI research fellow at the Foundation for Defense of Democracy in October. “They’ve taken a lot of bold moves in kind of lowering the hurdles in procurement for AI tools… I think it was a really great approach. That being said, I think the intense cultural pressure coming from the top down, of use AI and we’re, you know, putting out AI slop posts that say, ‘We’re an AI-first workforce’ is a lot because leading technical transformation in government, it’s often largely a cultural process. You have to get people to trust the tools that they’re using, and you have to get them comfortable with this.”
But without a structured approach to vetting what AI tools Airmen are using for what tasks, risks abound. “My biggest concern with the kind of pace we’re adopting AI is it’s actually going to expedite bad processes,” Siskind said.
Keeping a Close Watch
Retired USAF Lt. Gen. William Bender, former Air Force CIO, told Air & Space Forces Magazine he thinks the Department of the Air Force has good intentions, but he questions their ability to manage AI use at an enterprise level.
“Two things can be true at once: we’re measuring it, we’re watching it, and setting objectives and … it’s completely out of control,” Bender said.
Bender, who advises Kosmoy, a company that builds enterprise AI infrastructure and governance platforms, said that institutions should have governance controls in place before they push widespread use of AI tools. With any new technology, users may be inclined to find and adopt their own solutions rather than wait for the institution to certify specific solutions.
The result is what IT professionals call “shadow IT,” which are IT processes that the IT leaders can’t track or protect. He’d like to see the department adopt an enterprise tool to manage and track AI usage.
“Otherwise, it’s a formula for disaster if you don’t really know how it’s being managed,” Bender said.
Shadow IT or shadow AI use poses more than just risk. It carries costs that disappear in operational budgets but add up across the enterprise. “The Air Force has so much IT that was never headquartered-sanctioned, and yet it’s still costing the Air Force,” he said. “So, it’s one of the biggest problems in managing a finite IT budget, because you don’t know where most of it is. And there’s heavy reliance on some of the shadow stuff that was never sanctioned in the first place.” While Bender sees value in bottom-up innovation where Airmen use AI tools to solve real operational problems, the management challenge is to provide a top-down approach to control and protect data and networks.
“I would be looking for efficiencies and productivity by enabling AI to automate and drive an enablement of changed business practices and workflows inside of a constrained environment,” Bender said.
Both Bender and George Dougherty, a retired Air Force colonel and the author of “Beast in the Machine: How Robotics and AI Will Transform Warfare and the Future of Human Conflict,” see risk in unbounded use of the tools.
Army Acting CIO Gabe Chiulli announced in May “unlimited” AI access for Sage AI, a Defense Department platform for accessing various AI tools like OpenAI’s ChatGPT and Google’s Gemini. But usage far outstripped the budget. By mid-June, the Army had burned through its 100 million-token allotment for the year.
Constraints can be helpful to make people thing about efficient and effective use of resources.
DAF Chief Information Officer Ashely Devoto told Air & Space Forces Magazine in October that the department is already working on this.
For example, she said, running basic cybersecurity vulnerability checks might not require the top-of-the-line AI model, and instead could be accomplished with existing, non-AI tools.
“Start with your baseline scanner so that you’re not burning all the tokens identifying what a vulnerability scanner could have already identified,” Devoto said. “We’re trying to be thoughtful about the usage of these models that are going to get expensive very quickly.”
The department is working through usage questions for using AI tools and calculating compute requirements as DAF looks at how AI use will fit into its mid- and long-term budget planning.
Using Gemini, Grok, or ChatGPT for every search is “kind of like driving your Bentley everywhere,” Dougherty said. “If you were just going to go to the 7-Eleven and get a Slurpee, it doesn’t really make sense to take the Bentley there if you’ve got your Honda Civic.”
Usage and Tracking
The Department of the Air Force embraced DOD’s GenAI.mil platform earlier this year for unclassified and sensitive back-office tasks, such as budget planning. The platform provides access to Google Gemini, OpenAI’s ChatGPT, and xAI’s Grok.
To date, more than half the 3.3 million uniformed and civilian DOD personnel with access have used the platform, according to the Pentagon.
DAF Chief Data and Artificial Intelligence Officer Susan Davenport is responsible for AI strategy, policy, governance, oversight, and acceleration of AI capabilities within the department.
The department tracks “relevant use cases and capabilities” through a central inventory dubbed CLARA, an Air Force spokesperson told Air & Space Forces Magazine.
“These use cases are at different stages of maturity, ranging from evaluation and pilot efforts to more established operational applications,” the spokesperson said. “Access and use depend on mission need, security requirements, applicable approvals, and the sponsoring organization.”
The department’s goal is “pervasive, enterprise-wide adoption, supported by the DAF AI Strategy and the DAF AI Hiring & Talent Development Plan, which establishes the DAF as an AI-first force and mandates baseline AI literacy for all personnel.”
Wolfe, USAF’s top enlisted Airman, is doing his part to lead the charge. He established an AI Action Team, a widespread confederation of about 165 Airmen and Air Force civilians who meet virtually to identify “promising grassroots” AI projects for potential enterprise-level “visibility, support and adoption” for the broader Air Force, a lead member of the CMSAF’s AI Action Team told Air & Space Forces Magazine in an email response.
Wolfe’s staff did not disclose the names of any of the action team members. But speaking to Airmen at the conference in September, he invited them to bring their ideas and challenges to him and promised to connect them with task force members to help.
Among the more than 50 projects the team has brought to Wolfe’s attention so far are AI training for the 300-, 500-, and 700-level Air Force Foundation Course, beta testing for emerging DOD AI products, and building AI tools to streamline headquarters processes, the lead member wrote.
CMSAF and the team measure the utility of the tools by evaluating “project delivery, adoption, time and cost savings, process improvement, and the ability to scale successful solutions across the force,” the member wrote.
While Davenport’s CDAO office tracks the use cases and capabilities, responsibility for managing the development, authorization, and delivery of AI tools resides with the mission owners, the spokesperson wrote.
“A use case’s inclusion in the enterprise inventory does not itself constitute authorization for Department-wide use,” the spokesperson wrote.
The CDAO and DAF Data and AI Council provide oversight.
DAF evaluates whether AI tools being used for various missions support those mission outcomes via its AI Strategy.
Learning and Risks
Even when Airmen or Guardians use AI for routine office tasks or promotion board reviews, Bender said, unintentional risks remain.
Users could expose private information unwittingly through an errant prompt, he said. Or a user may ask the AI tool to perform a task, but the prompt may be interpreted differently than intended.
“Exposure to the internet is exposure to the world,” Bender said. “That also opens up-doors into your own networks that would otherwise have been potentially constrained.”
Air Force Maj. Megan Hainline, chief of air superiority programs in the International Affairs Weapons Division on the Air Staff and a visiting fellow at the Foundation for Defense of Democracy, said in a panel discussion in October that AI adoption will ultimately come Airman by Airman and unit by unit.
“There’s a lot of resources out there, but actually trickling that into the unit level and having somebody walk you through it” takes time, she said. People are busy, and may not be inclined to adopt tasks without a push, Hainline added: “It’s hard to take a step back and get to learn about these new technologies until it is kind of forced upon you.”
She advocates for squadron-level units to designate unit experts who can take the lead, updating and advising colleagues on tools specific to their jobs and duties and courses or videos for training.
“Give them a foothold, because it is overwhelming,” she said. “If you’re like, ‘I want to learn about AI,’ you have no idea where to start.”

articles.title: UK to fly RAF missions defending Saudi against Houthi attacks
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
UK to fly RAF missions defending Saudi Arabia against Houthi attacks
Britain will deploy Royal Air Force fighter jets on defensive missions to help protect Saudi Arabia from escalating Houthi attacks, Bloomberg reported on Tuesday, citing British officials familiar with the matter.
RAF Typhoon fighter jets will help defend Saudi cities and infrastructure against aerial attacks by the Iran-backed group, while Britain will also provide an Atlas A400M transport aircraft and military advisers, the report said.
Britain's Ministry of Defence did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
In September Britain said it would provide additional defensive military assistance to Saudi Arabia following renewed Houthi attacks, including an RAF Voyager air-to-air refuelling aircraft. That announcement did not include fighter jet support.
Houthi attacks have intensified in Saudi Arabia in recent weeks, with Yemen authorities saying on Monday that a strike on a government security forces training camp had killed 58 people.
